206881.extract: East Riddlesden Hall is a 17th-century manor house in Keighley, West Yorkshire, England, now owned by the National Trust.

'''East Riddlesden Hall''' is a 17th-century [[manor house]] in [[Keighley]], [[West Yorkshire]], England, now owned by the [[National Trust]].

==History==
The hall was built in 1642 by a wealthy [[Halifax, West Yorkshire|Halifax]] [[Cloth merchant|clothier]], James [[Murgatroyd]]. The hall is a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref>{{NHLE|num=1283478|grade=I|desc=East Riddlesden Hall|access-date=28 December 2016}}</ref> There is a [[medieval]] [[tithebarn]] in the grounds.

East Riddlesden Hall perches on a small plateau overlooking a bend in the [[River Aire]] on its way downstream from the town of [[Keighley]]. Interesting features include well-restored living accommodation on two floors, two [[White Rose of York|Yorkshire]] [[Rose windows]], walled garden, the ruined Starkie wing and several [[ghosts]] (reputedly).

The property was extended and re-built by James Murgatroyd and his wife Hannah, using local Yorkshire stone, in 1648. He also built other stone manor houses throughout the [[West Riding of Yorkshire]]. In the [[great hall]], a small fireplace can be seen above the main fireplace, where the floor for the first floor accommodation was not built. James Murgatroyd was a [[Cavalier|Royalist]] and this can be seen in royalist symbols and graffiti on and in the building. For example, the Bothy (now the tea room and shop) has the heads of [[Charles I of England]] and [[Henrietta Maria of France]] carved in the topmost stone work.

According to a [[National Operatic and Dramatic Association]] news feature in 2007, the Murgatroyd family are reputed to have been the inspiration for the Murgatroyd [[Baronet]]s in the [[comic opera]] ''[[Ruddigore]]'' by [[Gilbert and Sullivan]], and the opera has been performed at the Hall. [[W. S. Gilbert]] is supposed to have often stayed at the Hall. The feature comments that the Murgatroyds became notorious "for their profanity and [[:wikt:debauchery|debauchery]]". A legend arose that the River Aire changed its course in shame, in order to flow further away from the hall and its occupants (the river sweeps into a wide U-bend to skirt the meadow, as though giving the building a wide berth). The feature continues "Members of the family were fined, imprisoned and [[excommunicated]]". It asserts that the character of Sir Despard Murgatroyd in ''Ruddigore'' is based on James Murgatroyd.<ref>National Operatic and Dramatic Association, "Ruddigore: Close Up and Personal with Gilbert's Ghosts", NODA National News, vol. 65, no. 3, Autumn 2007, pp. 24 and 25</ref>

== Filming location ==
East Riddlesden Hall has been used as a [[filming location]] for the 1992 film ''[[Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights]]''<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0104181/locations |title=Filming locations for Wuthering Heights (1992) |publisher=The Internet Movie Database |access-date=16 January 2008 }}</ref> and for the 2009 TV adaptation.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1238834/locations  |title=Filming locations for Wuthering Heights (2009) |publisher=The Internet Movie Database |access-date=20 November 2011}}</ref> It was also used in ''[[Sharpe's Justice]]'' episode from the [[Sharpe (TV series)|Sharpe TV series]] in 1997.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0120109/locations |title=Filming locations for Sharpe's Justice (1997) (TV) |publisher=The Internet Movie Database |access-date=16 January 2008}}</ref> The [[BBC Television]] series '[[Gunpowder (TV series)|Gunpowder]]' (2017) used East Riddlesden Hall as a location.<ref name="hordley">{{cite web|last1=Hordley|first1=Chris|title=Where was BBC's Gunpowder Filmed?|url=http://www.creativeengland.co.uk/story/Where-BBC-Gunpowder-filmed|publisher=[[Creative England]]|access-date=29 November 2017|date=20 October 2017}}</ref>

226940.title: Wharfedale
226940.extract:
Wharfedale ( WHORF-dayl) is one of the Yorkshire Dales. It is situated at source in North Yorkshire and then flows into West Yorkshire and forms the upper valley of the River Wharfe. Towns and villages in Wharfedale (downstream, from west to east) include Buckden, Kettlewell, Conistone, Grassington, Hebden, Bolton Abbey, Addingham, Ilkley, Burley-in-Wharfedale, Otley, Pool-in-Wharfedale, Arthington, Collingham and Wetherby. Beyond Wetherby, the valley opens out and becomes part of the Vale of York.
The section from the river's source to around Addingham is known as Upper Wharfedale. It lies in North Yorkshire and the Yorkshire Dales National Park. The first 15 miles (24 km) or so is known as Langstrothdale, including the settlements of Beckermonds, Yockenthwaite and Hubberholme, famous for its church, the resting place of the writer J. B. Priestley. As it turns southwards, the Wharfe then runs through a green and lush valley, with limestone outcrops, such as Kilnsey Crag, and woodland, generally quite unusual in the Dales.
Below Addingham, the dale broadens and turns to the east. This section is shared between North Yorkshire and West Yorkshire and includes the towns of Ilkley, Otley and Wetherby. The northern side of Lower Wharfedale, opposite Ilkley, Burley-in-Wharfedale and Otley, is in the Nidderdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
The Yorkshire Dales Rivers Trust has a remit to conserve the ecological condition of Wharfedale, Wensleydale, Swaledale and Nidderdale catchments from their headwaters to the Humber Estuary.

'''Wharfedale''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|hw|ɔːr|f|d|eɪ|l}} {{respell|WHORF|dayl}}) is one of the [[Yorkshire Dales]]. It is situated at source in [[North Yorkshire]] and then flows into [[West Yorkshire]] and forms the upper valley of the [[River Wharfe]]. Towns and villages in Wharfedale (downstream, from west to east) include [[Buckden, North Yorkshire|Buckden]],{{efn|{{coord|54.191|-2.091|display=inline|region:GB_scale:10000}}}} [[Kettlewell]], [[Conistone]], [[Grassington]], [[Hebden, North Yorkshire|Hebden]], [[Bolton Abbey, North Yorkshire|Bolton Abbey]], [[Addingham]], [[Ilkley]], [[Burley-in-Wharfedale]], [[Otley]], [[Pool-in-Wharfedale]], [[Arthington]], [[Collingham, West Yorkshire|Collingham]] and [[Wetherby]].{{efn|{{coord|53.928|-1.386|display=inline|region:GB_scale:10000}}}} Beyond Wetherby, the valley opens out and becomes part of the [[Vale of York]].

The section from the river's source to around Addingham is known as ''Upper Wharfedale''. It lies in [[North Yorkshire]] and the [[Yorkshire Dales National Park]]. The first {{convert|15|mi|km}} or so is known as [[Langstrothdale]], including the settlements of [[Beckermonds]], [[Yockenthwaite]] and [[Hubberholme]], famous for its church, the resting place of the writer [[J. B. Priestley]]. As it turns southwards, the Wharfe then runs through a green and lush valley, with [[limestone]] [[outcrop]]s, such as [[Kilnsey|Kilnsey Crag]], and woodland, generally quite unusual in the Dales.

Below Addingham, the dale broadens and turns to the east. This section is shared between North Yorkshire and [[West Yorkshire]] and includes the towns of Ilkley, Otley and Wetherby. The northern side of Lower Wharfedale, opposite Ilkley, Burley-in-Wharfedale and Otley, is in the [[Nidderdale AONB|Nidderdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]].

The [[Yorkshire Dales Rivers Trust]] has a remit to conserve the ecological condition of Wharfedale, [[Wensleydale]], [[Swaledale]] and [[Nidderdale]] catchments from their headwaters to the [[Humber]] Estuary.

==History==
[[File:Otley Panorama.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|right|Lower Wharfedale from above [[Otley]]]]
The Wharfedale valley was cut into the shape we know today during the last ice age (the [[Last Glacial Period#Devensian and Midlandian glaciation (Britain and Ireland)|Devensian Glaciation]]). The valley was transformed into its classic U-shaped state between 18,000 and 12,000 years ago by the Wharfedale Glacier,<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Embleton |editor1-first=Clifford |title=Geomorphology of Europe |date=1994 |publisher=Macmillan |location=London |isbn=978-1-349-17346-4 |page=172}}</ref> though this was cutting through a channel that had already had a river draining water away to the east through what is now Wharfedale,<ref>{{cite web |title=Out of Oblivion: A landscape through time |url=http://www.outofoblivion.org.uk/geology.asp |website=www.outofoblivion.org.uk |access-date=5 January 2020 |archive-date=27 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727235149/http://www.outofoblivion.org.uk/geology.asp |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=18,000 YEARS AGO: THE WHARFEDALE GLACIER |url=https://www.wyorksgeologytrust.org/misc/Otley%20Interpretation%20Board.pdf |website=wyorksgeologytrust.org |access-date=5 January 2020}}</ref> and also to the north through what is now [[Bishopdale, North Yorkshire|Bishopdale]] and then [[Wensleydale]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Smithson |first1=Peter |last2=Addison |first2=Ken |last3=Atkinson |first3=Ken |title=Fundamentals of the physical environment |date=2002 |publisher=Routledge |location=London |isbn=0-415-23293-7 |page=5 |edition=3}}</ref> 

Evidence of human settlement has been found dating back to [[Neolithic]] times and the valley has plenty of artefacts relating to the [[Celtic Britons|Celtic]], [[Roman period|Roman]] and [[Anglo-Saxon period|Anglo-Saxon]] periods.<ref>{{cite web |title=Out of Oblivion: A landscape through time |url=http://www.outofoblivion.org.uk/upwharfedale.asp |website=www.outofoblivion.org.uk |access-date=5 January 2020 |archive-date=19 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190419211416/http://www.outofoblivion.org.uk/upwharfedale.asp |url-status=dead }}</ref> The Romans built a road over Stake Moss into what is now the village of [[Bainbridge, North Yorkshire|Bainbridge]] in Wensleydale.<ref>{{cite web |title=YORKSHIRE DALES NATIONAL PARK LANDSCAPE CHARACTER ASSESSMENT |url=https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/2019/09/LCA-combined-files-final-report.pdf |website=yorkshiredales.org.uk |access-date=5 January 2020 |page=115}}</ref> 

The Anglo-Saxon influence remains in modern times, with most settlements in Upper Wharfedale having Anglo-Saxon derived names.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Harker |first1=Bailey John |title=Rambles in upper Wharfedale; including the historical and traditional lore of the district |date=1869 |publisher=Pitman |location=London |page=288|oclc=931181143}}</ref>

The name of the valley is derived from the principal river that flows through it: the Wharfe, which comes from the [[Old English]] ''Weorf'' or [[Old Norse]] ''Hverfr'', with both taken as meaning ''winding river''.<ref>{{cite web |title=River Wharfe |url=http://www.yorkshiredalesriverstrust.com/your-rivers/river-wharfe/ |website=yorkshiredalesriverstrust.com |access-date=5 January 2020}}</ref> The River Wharfe starts at the confluence (at the hamlet of Beckermonds) of the Oughtershaw Beck and the Green Field Beck,<ref>Ordnance Survey maps</ref> each of which originates at the Pennine watershed, some {{convert|6|km|0|order=flip}} north-east of [[Ribblehead]]. The valley roughly follows a south-easterly direction, providing a border between West Yorkshire (on the south side) and North Yorkshire.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lower Wharfedale National Mapping Project |url=https://research.historicengland.org.uk/redirect.aspx?id=6862%7CWest%20Yorkshire%20Lower%20Wharfedale%20NMP%20Project%20Summary%20Report%20(2957) |website=research.historicengland.org.uk |access-date=5 January 2020 |page=5 |format=PDF |date=2004}}</ref> 

Between Oughtershaw Moss and Wetherby, the valley runs for {{convert|50|mi}}.<ref name="YGS">{{cite journal |last1=Raistrick |first1=A. |title=The Glaciation of Wharfedale, Yorkshire |journal=Proceedings of the Yorkshire Geological Society |date=1931 |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=9–30 |doi=10.1144/pygs.22.1.9 |publisher=Yorkshire Geological Society}}</ref> The uppermost part of the valley is known as Langstrothdale.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Buckley |first1=Norman |title=Yorkshire Dales walking : on the level |date=2004 |publisher=Sigma Leisure |location=Wilmslow |isbn=1-85058-439-7 |page=29}}</ref> Below Beckermonds the river is known as the River Wharfe.<ref>{{cite map|title =Yorkshire Dales - Southern & Western Area |map =OL2|year =2015 |scale =1:25,000 |series =Explorer |publisher =Ordnance Survey |isbn =9780319263310 }}</ref> Wetherby is traditionally seen as the foot of Wharfedale, even though the river continues on through the [[Vale of York]].<ref name="YGS"/>

The valley has been used largely for agriculture, and is now criss-crossed with stone walls and stone barns that evidence its use down the centuries.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davies |first1=Carey |title=Country diary: Wharfedale, Yorkshire: A glacier bored out the contours of this valley, but the detail was added by hand |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/may/04/glacier-contours-valley-wharfedale-yorkshire |access-date=5 January 2020 |work=The Guardian |date=4 May 2014}}</ref>

==Geology==
The geology of the valley is split, with Upper Wharfedale consisting of [[carboniferous limestone]] of the [[Yoredale]] series.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Speight |first1=Harry |title=Upper Wharfedale : being a complete account of the history, antiquities and scenery of the picturesque valley of the Wharfe, from Otley to Langstrothdale |date=1900 |publisher=E Stock |location=London |page=20|oclc=1079273371}}</ref> In the lower part of Wharfedale, around [[Ilkley]] and [[Otley]], the underlying stone is mostly millstone grit,<ref>{{cite web |title=Geology |url=http://www.wharfedale-nats.org.uk/geology/ |website=wharfedale-nats.org.uk |access-date=5 January 2020 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> which can be seen best at the Cow and Calf rocks on the south side of the valley on [[Ilkley Moor]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davies |first1=Carey |title=People have been leaving their marks on these rocks since the bronze age |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/feb/05/marks-rocks-since-bronze-age-ilkley-yorkshire |access-date=5 January 2020 |work=The Guardian |date=5 February 2018}}</ref> The Bramley Almanac for 1931 lists 'Earthquake in Wharfedale' for 15 December 1859.<ref>The Bramley Almanac for 1931 (publ. William Witts, Town Street, Bramley)</ref>

==Wharfedale Ward==
As an [[electoral]] subdivision Wharfedale is a [[Ward (politics)|ward]] in the north east of the [[City of Bradford]] [[metropolitan borough]]. It consists of the settlements of [[Burley-in-Wharfedale]], [[Burley Woodhead]] and [[Menston]] along with surrounding moorland. The population of the ward taken at the 2011 Census was 11,836.<ref>{{NOMIS2011|id=E05001366|title=Wharfedale Ward (as of 2011)|access-date=5 January 2020}}</ref>

==Deanery of South Craven and Wharfedale==
{{Main|Craven District#South Craven and Wharfedale}}
In 2017, in consideration of [[regional geography]], the [[Church of England]] changed its subdivisions<ref>[http://www.westyorkshiredales.anglican.org/content/maps-and-information-about-deaneries-and-parishes Maps of Anglican deaneries and parishes.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727235010/https://www.westyorkshiredales.anglican.org/content/maps-and-information-about-deaneries-and-parishes |date=27 July 2020 }} Retrieved 6 May 2017</ref> and re-grouped the [[Deanery]] of Wharfedale with that of [[Craven District#Deanery of South Craven|South Craven]], in order that the similar regions can work together more effectively.<ref name="anglican">[http://www.westyorkshiredales.anglican.org/news/bradford-episcopal-map-redrawn-new-area-deans-announced West Yorkshire Dales Anglican News.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728022902/https://www.westyorkshiredales.anglican.org/news/bradford-episcopal-map-redrawn-new-area-deans-announced |date=28 July 2020 }} Retrieved 6 May 2017</ref>

==Wharfedale in culture==
[[File:John Atkinson Grimshaw - Wharfedale 1872.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|[[John Atkinson Grimshaw]] – Wharfedale 1872]]
One of the most renowned painters of the Victorian era, [[John Atkinson Grimshaw]], portrayed the area in his piece, "Moonlight, Wharfedale" (1871 – oil on card {{convert|17+1/2|x|13+1/2|inch|cm|disp=sqbr}}). He is known as one of the best and most accomplished nightscape and townscape artists of all time, and this painting is a prime example of his mastery.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://fineartamerica.com/featured/john-atkinson-grimshaw-moonlight-wharfedale-1871-motionage-designs.html|title=John Atkinson Grimshaw Moonlight Wharfedale 1871 by MotionAge Designs|website=Fine Art America|access-date=19 December 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.artnet.com/artists/john-atkinson-grimshaw/moonlight-wharfedale-pVibVPIS7PQGOYFQjklbZw2|title=Moonlight Wharfedale by John AtkinsonGrimshaw|website=www.artnet.com|access-date=19 December 2018}}</ref> [[J. M. W. Turner]] also visited and painted scenes around Otley and Ilkley. Turner was commissioned to paint [[Kilnsey|Kilnsey Crag]], which he created as an oil painting in 1816.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ames |first1=Daryl |title=Artist enlists local help to recreate Turner scene |url=https://www.cravenherald.co.uk/news/9852637.artist-enlists-local-help-to-recreate-turner-scene/ |access-date=5 January 2020 |work=Craven Herald |date=2 August 2012 }}</ref>

The valley was featured in episode three of the [[BBC Two]] series, ''The Yorkshire Dales''.<ref>{{cite web |title=BBC Two – The Yorkshire Dales, Series 1, Wharfedale |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m0004c12 |website=BBC |access-date=5 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Chandler |first1=Stuart |title=All you need to know about new BBC Two documentary The Yorkshire Dales |url=https://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/best-in-yorkshire/outdoors/all-you-need-to-know-about-new-bbc-two-documentary-the-yorkshire-dales-1-9772978 |access-date=5 January 2020 |work=The Yorkshire Post |date=16 May 2019 |url-access=limited}}</ref>

782410.title: Roseberry Topping
782410.extract:
Roseberry Topping is a distinctive hill in North Yorkshire, England. It is situated near Great Ayton and Newton under Roseberry. Its summit has a distinctive half-cone shape with a jagged cliff, which has led to many comparisons with the much higher Matterhorn in the Swiss-Italian Alps. It is a symbol of the area and features in the logo of the nearby Teesside International Airport.
At 1,049 feet (320 m), Roseberry Topping was traditionally thought to be the highest hill on the North York Moors but there are 15 higher peaks, with the nearby Urra Moor being the highest, at 1,490 feet (450 m). Roseberry Topping offers views of Captain Cook's Monument on Easby Moor and the monument on Eston Nab, previously a beacon.

main.*:
{{Short description|Prominent hill and landmark in North Yorkshire, England}} {{Use British English|date=June 2020}} {{Use dmy dates|date=June 2016}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Roseberry Topping | image = Roseberry topping north side.jpg | image_caption = Roseberry Topping from the north | elevation_m = 320 | elevation_ref = | prominence_m = 81 | prominence_ref = | listing = | location = [[North York Moors]], [[England]] | range = | map = United Kingdom North Yorkshire | map_caption = Roseberry Topping within [[North Yorkshire]] | map_size = | label_position = right | coordinates = {{coord|54.50542|N|1.10736|W|type:mountain_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | grid_ref_UK = NZ579126 | topo = [[Ordnance Survey|OS]] ''Landranger'' 193 | type = | first_ascent = | easiest_route = }} '''Roseberry Topping''' is a distinctive [[hill]] in [[North Yorkshire]], [[England]]. It is situated near [[Great Ayton]] and [[Newton under Roseberry]]. Its summit has a distinctive half-cone shape with a jagged [[cliff]], which has led to many comparisons with the much higher [[Matterhorn]] in the [[Italy-Switzerland border|Swiss-Italian Alps]].Howard Peach, ''Curious Tales of Old North Yorkshire'', p. 39 (Sigma Leisure, 2004) It is a symbol of the area and features in the logo of the nearby [[Teesside International Airport]].{{cite web |url=https://www.gazettelive.co.uk/news/teesside-news/teesside-airport-gets-name-back-16644428 |title=Teesside Airport gets its name back - and connections to London, Dublin and Belfast could be next|access-date=31 January 2020 |work=Teesside Live Website |date=25 July 2019}}{{cite web |url=https://www.teessideinternational.com/welcome-to-tees-valley/ |title=Welcome to Tees Valley|access-date=31 January 2020 |work=Teesside International Airport Website }} At {{convert|1049|ft|m}}, Roseberry Topping was traditionally thought to be the highest hill on the [[North York Moors]]See e.g. J. J. Sheahan and T. Whellan, ''[https://archive.org/details/historyandtopog00cogoog History and Topography of the City of York; the Ainsty Wapentake; and the East Riding of Yorkshire]'', p. 10. 1855. but there are 15 higher peaks, with the nearby [[Urra Moor]] being the highest, at {{convert|1490|ft|}}. Roseberry Topping offers views of Captain Cook's Monument on [[Easby Moor]] and the monument on [[Eston Nab]], previously a beacon. ==Geology== The hill is an outlier of the [[North York Moors]] uplands. It is formed from [[sandstone]] laid down in the [[Middle Jurassic|Middle]] and [[Lower Jurassic]] periods, between 208 and 165 million years ago, which constitutes the youngest sandstone to be found in any of the national parks in England and Wales. Its distinctive conical shape is the result of the hill's hard sandstone cap protecting the underlying [[shale]]s and [[clay]]s from erosion by the effects of ice, wind and rain.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} Until 1912 the summit resembled a [[sugarloaf]], until a [[geological fault]] and possibly nearby [[alum]] and [[Cleveland Ironstone Formation|ironstone]] mining caused it to collapse. The area immediately below the summit is still extensively pitted and scarred from the former mineworks. From the summit there are magnificent views across the Cleveland plain as far as the [[Pennines]] on a clear day, some {{convert|40–50|mi}} away.{{cite news |title=The '˜Yorkshire Matterhorn' that inspired Cook |url=https://www.yorkshireeveningpost.co.uk/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/yorkshire-matterhorn-inspired-cook-620307 |access-date=12 August 2022 |work=Yorkshire Evening Post |date=15 May 2016}}{{cite news |last1=Johnstone |first1=Charlotte |title=Why you must visit the picturesque Yorkshire village where Captain Cook grew up |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/destinations/europe/united-kingdom/articles/great-british-getaways-great-ayton/ |access-date=12 August 2022 |work=The Telegraph |date=22 August 2018|url-access=subscription}} ==History== [[File:Rj roseberry topping.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|Aerial photo]] [[File:Roseberry Topping hoard.jpg|right|thumb|upright=1.4|Replicas of the Bronze Age Roseberry Topping hoard]] The Roseberry area has been inhabited for thousands of years and the hill has long attracted attention for its distinctive shape. A [[Bronze Age]] hoard was discovered on the slopes of the hill and is now in the [[Sheffield City Museum]]. It was occupied during the [[Iron Age]]: walled enclosures and the remains of huts dating from the period are still visible in the vicinity of the hill. During this period [[Jet (gemstone)|Jet]] may have been mined in the area.{{cite book |last=Muller |first=Helen |date=1987 |title=Jet|publisher=Butterworths |page=11 |isbn=0408031107}} The hill may have been held in special regard by the [[Vikings]] who settled in [[Cleveland, Yorkshire|Cleveland]] during the early [[medieval]] period and gave the area many of its place names. They gave Roseberry Topping its present name: first attested in 1119 as Othenesberg, its second element is accepted to derive from Old Norse ''bjarg'' (rock) and the first element must be an Old Norse personal name, Authunn or Óthinn, giving 'Authunn's/Óthinn's rock'. If the latter, Roseberry Topping is one of only a handful of known pagan names in England, being named after the [[Norse mythology|Norse]] god [[Odin]] and paralleled by the Old English name ''Wodnesberg'', found for example in [[Woodnesborough]], or Woden Law.Victor Watts (ed.), ''The Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names Based on the Collections of the English Place-Name Society'' (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2004), s.v. ROSEBERRY TOPPING; Peter Godfrey Foote, Hans Bekker-Nielsen, Olaf Olsen. ''Proceedings of the Eighth Viking Congress: Århus 24–31 August 1977'', p. 135. Odense University Press, 1981. {{ISBN|87-7492-339-0}} The name changed successively to Othensberg, Ohenseberg, Ounsberry and Ouesberry before finally settling on Roseberry. ‘Topping’ is a Yorkshire dialectal derivation of Old English ''topp'', top (of a hill).A. H. Smith, ''English Place-Name Elements'', 2 vols, English Place-Name Society, 25–26 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1956), s.v. ''topping''. The naming of the hill may thus fit a well-established pattern in Continental Europe of hills and mountains being named after Odin or the Germanic equivalent, Wodan. [[Ælfric of Eynsham|Aelfric of Eynsham]], writing in the 10th century, recorded how "the heathens made him into a celebrated god and made offerings to him at crossroads and brought [[oblation]]s to high hills for him. This god was honoured among all heathens and he is called ... Othon in Danish."[[Ken Dowden]], ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=b-QfhYxtKScC European Paganism: The Realities of Cult from Antiquity to the Middle Ages]'', p. 80. Routledge, 2000. {{ISBN|0-415-12034-9}} In 1736, explorer [[James Cook]]'s family moved to Airey Holme Farm at nearby [[Great Ayton]]. When he had time off from working on the farm with his father, young James took himself off up Roseberry Topping, which gave him his first taste for adventure and exploration, which was to stay with him for life. Roseberry Topping can be seen from many miles away and was long used by sailors and farmers as an indicator of impending bad weather. An old rhyme commemorates this usage: :''When Roseberry Topping wears a cap, let Cleveland then beware of a clap!''G. F. Northall, ''English Folk Rhymes 1892'', p. 91 The hill was private property for many years, formerly being part of a game estate owned by the Cressy family.{{citation needed|date=February 2026}} In the early 18th century, Dorothea Cressy married [[Archibald Primrose, 1st Earl of Rosebery|Archibald Primrose]], who was later made [[Earl of Rosebery]]. Roseberry Topping is now managed by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and is open to the public. It is just within the [[North York Moors National Park]], the border of which runs along the [[A173 road]] below it.{{cite book |editor1-last=Pearce |editor1-first=Ian |title=Roseberry Topping |date=2006 |publisher=Great Ayton Community Archaeology Project |location=Great Ayton |isbn=978-0-9554153-0-2 |page=141 |chapter=17: Roseberry on historic maps}} A spur of the [[Cleveland Way]] [[National Trail]] runs up to the summit. The path has been a sightseeing excursion route for centuries owing to the views of the Cleveland area from the summit: as early as 1700 travellers were recommended to visit the peak to see "the most delightful prospect upon the valleys below to the hills above."''Brome's Travels'', vol. 8. London, 1700 The site was [[SSSI notification|notified]] as a [[geological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in 1954, with a boundary extension in 1986 bringing the designated area to 10.86 [[hectare]]s. The site is listed as being of national importance in the [[Geological Conservation Review]].{{cite web |url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1000120.pdf |title=SSSI citation sheet for Roseberry Topping|access-date=15 February 2007 |work=English Nature }} During the Napoleonic Wars, the Wensleydale volunteers responded to a false alarm when the beacon on [[Penhill]], in Wensleydale, [[North Yorkshire]] was lit in response to a supposed lit beacon on Roseberry Topping, 40 miles distant. It turned out to be burning heather.{{cite book|last=Pontefract|first=Ella|author-link=Ella Pontefract|title=Wensleydale|location=London|publisher=Dent|year=1936|page=176}} ==In popular culture== In [[Joseph Reed (playwright)|Joseph Reed]]'s 1761 farce ''The Register-Office'', the character Margery Moorpout, who hails from 'Yatton', sings the praises of 'Roseberry', which she claims to be a mile and a half high:
''Certainly God! ye knaw Roseberry? I thought ony Fule had knawn Roseberry!—It's t' biggest Hill in oll ''Yorkshire''—It's aboun a Mile an a hofe high, an as coad as Ice at' top on't i't hettest Summer's Day—that it's.''Joseph Reed (1771), ''The register-office: a farce of two acts. Acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane. By Joseph Reed. A new edition.'' London: T. Davies and T. Becket and Co. ECCO Print Editions. ESTCID: T064222 [Reproduction from British Library], p. 14
In 1783, Thomas Pierson, a blacksmith, watchmaker and schoolmaster from the nearby town of [[Stokesley]], wrote an eponymous poem about the hill. Pierson's work was much admired locally and it was republished in 1847.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HbksAQAAMAAJ|title=Roseberry Topping: A Poem. (Originally Pub. 1783). With Notes, and Also a Notice of the Author and a Memoir of the Late Thomas Jennett|first=Thomas|last=Pierson|date=18 June 1847|publisher=Jennett|via=Google Books}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Roseberry Topping}} * [https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/roseberry-topping Roseberry Topping information at the National Trust] * [https://www.visitgreatayton.com/what-to-do-in-great-ayton/walk/roseberry-topping Roseberry Topping trail routes at Visit Great Ayton] {{SSSIs Cleveland}} {{Hills and moors of the North York Moors}} [[Category:Mountains and hills of North Yorkshire]] [[Category:National Trust properties in North Yorkshire]] [[Category:Sites of Special Scientific Interest in Cleveland, England]] [[Category:North York Moors]] [[Category:Great Ayton]]

'''Robin Hood's Bay''' is a village in [[North Yorkshire]], England. It is {{Convert|6|mi|km|0}} south of [[Whitby]] and {{Convert|15|mi|km}} north of [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire|Scarborough]] on the [[Yorkshire Coast]]. Robin Hood's Bay is a tourist destination in the [[North York Moors National Park]].

It is an ancient [[chapelry]] of [[Fylingdales]] in the [[wapentake]] of [[Whitby Strand]]. It is on the [[Cleveland Way]] national trail and also the end point of Wainwright's [[Coast to Coast Walk|Coast to Coast]] route.

== History ==
[[File:(Whitby, Robin Hood's Bay, Yorkshire, England) (LOC) (16180464504).jpg|thumb|"Whitby, Robin Hood's Bay, Yorkshire, England", {{circa|1890–1900}}]]

=== Toponymy ===
The origin of the name is uncertain, and it is doubtful that [[Robin Hood]] was ever in the vicinity of the village (if indeed he ever existed). The place is attested in the early sixteenth century as "Robyn Hoodis Baye" in 1544.<!-- I cannot actually find the reference, but it's allegedly in Volume 19, no. 1 of the ''Letters and Papers of Henry VIII'', p. 224.  But I'm not seeing it there, so failed citation?--> The English ballad ''[[The Noble Fisherman]]'' tells a story of Robin Hood visiting [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire|Scarborough]], taking a job as a fisherman, defeating French [[pirate]]s with his archery skills, and using half the looted treasure to build a home for the poor.  However, the ballad is only attested to in the 17th century at the earliest. It is considered more likely to be a work original to the 17th century rather than an older medieval popular legend passed down, and very unlikely to be based on any historical incident. However, it is possible the author knew of Robin Hood's Bay, and sought to tie the story he wrote to the Scarborough area to explain and justify the name.<ref name="rymes">{{cite book |last1=Dobson |first1=R. B. |last2=Taylor |first2=J. |date=1997 |orig-date=1976 |title=Rymes of Robin Hood |url= |location= |publisher=Sutton |pages=179–182; 306 |isbn=0-7509-1661-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |year=2014 |title=Robin Hoods Bay |url=http://www.outdoorsoc.co.uk/venues.php?id=19 |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=The University of York Outdoor Society |archive-date=2 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002071102/http://www.outdoorsoc.co.uk/venues.php?id=19 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Early history ===
By about 1000 the neighbouring hamlet of [[Raw, North Yorkshire|Raw]] and the village of Thorpe (Fylingthorpe) in Fylingdales had been settled by [[Norway|Norwegians]] and [[Danes (Germanic tribe)|Danes]]. After the [[Norman conquest of England|Norman conquest]] in 1069 much land in [[Northern England]], including Fylingdales, was laid waste. [[William the Conqueror]] gave Fylingdales to Tancred the Fleming, who later sold it to the Abbot of Whitby.<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=12}}</ref>

In the period 1324–1346 there was an early reference to Robin Hood's Bay. Louis I, Count of Flanders, wrote a letter to [[Edward III of England|King Edward III]] in which he complained that Flemish fishermen together with their boats and catches were taken by force to Robyn Oeds Bay.<ref>{{Cite web |title=STORM AND COMPANY |url=http://freepages.rootsweb.com/~stormrhb/genealogy/flanders.htm |access-date=13 July 2019 |website=freepages.rootsweb.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=International Robin Hood Biography |url=https://www.irhb.org/wiki/index.php/1324_-_Louis,_count_of_Flanders_-_Letter_to_Edward_II_or_III}}</ref> The settlements were about a mile inland at Raw but by about 1500 a settlement had grown up on the coast. "Robin Hoode Baye" was mentioned by [[John Leland (antiquary)|Leland]] in 1536 who described it as,<ref name=vch />
{{quote|"A fischer tounlet of 20 bootes with Dok or Bosom of a mile yn length."<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=13}}</ref>}}
[[File:Fisher Folk in Robin Hood's Bay , 1880.png|thumb|left|upright|Fisher folk, Robin Hood's Bay, 1880, by Frank Sutcliffe]]
[[File:Globe at Robin Hoods Bay.JPG|thumb|right|Robin Hood's Bay Sculpture]]
After the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] in 1540, [[Whitby Abbey]] and its lands became the property of [[Henry VIII of England|King Henry VIII]] with King Street and King's Beck dating from this time.<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=16}}</ref>

In the 16th century, Robin Hood's Bay was a more important port than Whitby, it is described by a tiny picture of tall houses and an anchor on old [[North Sea]] charts published by [[Lucas Janszoon Waghenaer|Waghenaer]] in 1586 and now in [[Rotterdam]]'s Maritime Museum.<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=14}}</ref>

{{clear left}}

=== Smuggling ===
The village, which consists of a maze of tiny streets, has a tradition of [[smuggling]], and there is reputed to be a network of subterranean passageways linking the houses. During the late 18th century smuggling was rife on the Yorkshire coast. Vessels from the continent brought contraband which was distributed by contacts on land and the operations were financed by syndicates who made profits without the risks taken by the seamen and the villagers. Tea, gin, rum, brandy and tobacco were among the contraband smuggled into Yorkshire from the [[Netherlands]] and France to avoid the duty.<ref name="Farnill 1966 22">{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=22}}</ref>

In 1773 two excise cutters, the ''Mermaid'' and the ''Eagle'', were outgunned and chased out of the bay by three smuggling vessels, a schooner and two shallops.<ref name="Farnill 1966 22" />
A pitched battle between smugglers and excise men took place in the dock over 200 casks of brandy and geneva (gin) and 15 bags of tea in 1779.<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=34}}</ref>

=== Fishing, farming and lifeboats ===
[[File:Robin Hoods Bay Whitby North Yorkshire Fishing Beach.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|A boat in Robin Hood's Bay]]
Fishing and farming were the original occupations followed by generations of Bay folk. Many houses in the village were built between 1650 and 1750 and whole families were involved in the fishing industry. Many families owned or part-owned cobles. Later some owned ocean-going craft.<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=44}}</ref> Fishing reached its peak in the mid 19th century, fishermen used the [[coble]] for line fishing in winter and a larger boat for herring fishing. Fish was loaded into panniers and men and women walked or rode over the moorland tracks to [[Pickering, North Yorkshire|Pickering]] or [[York]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Farnill|1966|p=43}}</ref>

[[File:Closeup of The Visiter wreck plaque New Road Robin Hoods Bay Whitby North Yorkshire.jpg|thumb|The "Visitor" wreck plaque|left]]
A plaque in the village records that a [[brig]] named "Visiter" ran aground in Robin Hood's Bay on 18 January 1881 during a violent storm. In order to save the crew, the lifeboat from [[Whitby]] was pulled {{convert|6|mi}} overland by 18 horses, with the {{convert|7|ft|adj=on}} deep snowdrifts present at the time cleared by 200 men. The road down to the sea through Robin Hood's Bay village was narrow and had awkward bends, and men had to go ahead demolishing garden walls and uprooting bushes to make a way for the lifeboat carriage. It was launched two hours after leaving Whitby, with the crew of the "Visiter" rescued on the second attempt.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ravenscroft |first=John |year=2006 |title=Robin Hood's Bay: Fishing Hamlet, Smuggler's Haven |url=http://www.timetravel-britain.com/articles/towns/bay.shtml |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=timetravel-britain.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |year=2014 |title=Whitby Lifeboats |url=http://www.whitby-yorkshire.co.uk/lifeboat/lifeboats.htm |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=whitby-yorkshire.co.uk |archive-date=24 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224065734/http://www.whitby-yorkshire.co.uk/lifeboat/lifeboats.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The main legitimate activity had always been fishing, but this started to decline in the late 19th century. These days most of its income comes from tourism.<ref>{{cite web |last=Lidster |first=Robin |date=April 1998 |title=Heritage & History of Robin Hood's Bay |url=http://www.bayfair.co.uk/history.html |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=Bayfair}}</ref>

Robin Hood's Bay is also known for the large number of [[fossil]]s which may be found on its beach. The foreshore rocks on the north side of the bay, in particular, are a well known location for finding [[ammonites]], especially after winter storms.<ref>{{cite web |title=Robin Hoods Bay |url=https://ukfossils.co.uk/2007/03/18/robin-hoods-bay/ |website=UK Fossil Collecting |access-date=4 July 2021 |date=18 March 2007}}</ref>

In 1912, Professor [[Walter Garstang]] of [[Leeds University]], in cooperation with Professor Alfred Denny of the [[University of Sheffield]], established the [[Robin Hood's Bay Marine Laboratory]], which continued on the site for the next 71 years, closing in 1983.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mieszkowska |first1=N. |last2=Sugden |first2=H. |last3=Firth |first3=L. B. |last4=Hawkins |first4=S. J. |title=The role of sustained observations in tracking impacts of environmental change on marine biodiversity and ecosystems |journal=Philosophical Transactions: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |date=28 September 2014 |volume=372 |issue=2,025 |page=4 |publisher=Royal Society of London. |location=London |doi=10.1098/rsta.2013.0339 |pmid=25157190 |pmc=4150294 |bibcode=2014RSPTA.37230339M |issn=1364-503X}}</ref>

== Governance ==
Robin Hood's Bay was part of the chapelry of Fylingdales in the Liberty of Whitby Strand, which was a [[wapentake]] in the [[North Riding of Yorkshire]]. From 1974 to 2023 it was part of the [[Borough of Scarborough]]. It is now administered by the unitary [[North Yorkshire Council]].

== Geography ==
[[File:Robin Hoods Bay 1 (Nigel Coates).jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|New Road, leading down to the sea shore]]
Robin Hood's Bay is built in a fissure between two steep cliffs. The village houses were built mostly of [[sandstone]] with red-tiled roofs. The main street is New Road, which descends from the cliff-top where the manor house, the newer houses and [[St Stephen's Church, Fylingdales]] stand. It passes through the village crossing the King's Beck and reaches the beach by a cobbled slipway known as Wayfoot where the [[Stream|beck]] discharges onto the beach.

The cliffs are composed of Upper [[Lias Group|Lias]] [[shale]], capped by Dogger and False Bedded Sandstones and shales of the Lower [[Oolite]].<ref name="vch">{{Cite web |date=1923 |editor-last=Page |editor-first=William |title=Parishes: Fylingdales |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=64704 |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=A History of the County of York North Riding |publisher=Institute of Historical Research |volume=2}}</ref>

The ''Wine Haven Profile'' near Robin Hood's Bay is the Global Stratotype Section and Point ([[Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point|GSSP]]) of the [[Pliensbachian]] Epoch (183,0–189,6 mya), one of four chronographic substages of the [[Early Jurassic]] Epoch.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2013 |title=GSSP for Pliensbachian Stage |url=http://www.stratigraphy.org/GSSP/Pliensbachian.html |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=International Commission on Stratigraphy}}</ref>

The headlands at each end of the beach are known as Ness Point or North Cheek (north) and Old Peak or South Cheek (south).

== Transport ==
The village was once served by [[Robin Hood's Bay railway station]]<ref>{{cite web |year=2014 |title=Disused Stations: Robin Hoods Bay Station |url=http://www.disused-stations.org.uk/r/robin_hoods_bay/index.shtml |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=Subterranea Britannica}}</ref> on the [[Scarborough and Whitby Railway]] line which opened in 1885 and closed in 1965. The track of the old railway is now a footpath and cycleway. The nearest railway station is in [[Whitby railway station|Whitby]].

The village connects to the [[A171 road|A171]] allowing access to Whitby and [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire|Scarborough]]. The X93 Arriva bus service between Scarborough and [[Middlesbrough]] passes through Robin Hood's Bay every hour, increasing to every 30 minutes or every 20 minutes during the summer.<ref>{{cite web |year=2014 |title=X93 – Middlesbrough – Whitby – Robin Hoods Bay – Scarborough |url=http://www.arrivabus.co.uk/ServiceSearchResults.aspx?txt=x93&stype=service&reg=UK |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=[[Arriva Yorkshire]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Smith |first=Jonathan |date=19 April 2019 |title=Walks: Take an Easter stroll from Robin Hood's Bay to the fishing port of Whitby |work=Darlington and Stockton Times |url=https://www.darlingtonandstocktontimes.co.uk/news/17583358.walks-take-an-easter-stroll-from-robin-hoods-bay-to-the-fishing-port-of-whitby/ |access-date=16 August 2019}}</ref> 

Robin Hood's Bay is the eastern terminus of [[Alfred Wainwright|Wainwright]]'s [[Coast to Coast Walk]] that crosses from [[St Bees Head]] on the [[Irish Sea]] coast of [[Cumbria]]. The village is also on the coastal section of the [[Cleveland Way]], a long-distance footpath that encircles the [[North York Moors]], and the [[Cinder Track]], a multi-user path that forms part of [[National Cycle Route 1]] and links Whitby and Scarborough.

== Religion ==
[[File:St Stephens Church Robin Hoods Bay 4 (Nigel Coates).jpg|thumb|left|The new St Stephen's Church on Thorpe Lane]]
Robin Hood's Bay is in the parish of Fylingdales, which contains two churches both dedicated to St Stephen. The [[Old St Stephen's Church, Fylingdales]], on the hillside at Raw, above the village, replaced an ancient church which had [[Saxon]] origins and was demolished in about 1821. This was a dependent chapel of [[Whitby Abbey]]. A new church, also St Stephen's, designed by [[George Edmund Street]], was built in 1870.<ref name=vch />

The village was visited by the preacher [[John Wesley]] in 1761,<ref>North Yorkshire Coast Methodist Circuit in 1761, [https://northyorkscoastmethodist.org.uk/our-locations/ Churches], accessed on 8 November 2025</ref> and has a [[Methodist]] church.<ref>North Yorkshire Coast Methodist Circuit, [https://northyorkscoastmethodist.org.uk/our-locations/robin-hoods-bay-methodist-church/ Robin Hoods Bay Methodist Church], accessed on 8 November 2025</ref>
{{clear left}}

== Culture ==
[[File:The Bay Hotel, Robin Hood's Bay - geograph.org.uk - 1474424.jpg|thumb|left|[[The Bay Hotel]]]]

Robin Hood's Bay is the setting for the ''Bramblewick'' novels (''Three Fevers'', ''Phantom Lobster'', ''Foreigners,'' ''Sally Lunn, Master Mariner'' and ''Sound of the Sea'') by [[Leo Walmsley]] (1892–1966), who was educated in the schoolroom of the [[The Old Chapel, Robin Hood's Bay|old Wesleyan Chapel]], in the lower village. The 1935 film ''Turn of the Tide'', based on Walmsley's ''Three Fevers'', was filmed in the village.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turn of the Tide |website=[[IMDb]] |url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0027140/ |access-date=13 July 2019}}</ref>

In 1925, the [[Fylingdales Group of Artists]] was founded at Denton Hawley's studio in Robin Hood's Bay.<ref name="artbiogs">{{Cite web |title=Fylingdales Group |url=https://www.artbiogs.co.uk/2/societies/fylingdales-group |access-date=10 July 2020 |website=Artist Biographies – British and Irish Artists of the 20th Century |location=UK}}</ref>

In 1948, ''[[Life (magazine)|LIFE]]'' magazine ran a story of an unknown [[Poison pen letter|Poison Penman]] who had been writing spiteful anonymous letters to the inhabitants of Robin Hood's Bay since 1928.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=31 May 1948 |title=Vicar Exorcises a Poison Penman |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WkYEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA45 |magazine=[[Life (magazine)|LIFE]] |pages=45–46 |issn=0024-3019}}</ref>

The 2008 film ''[[Wild Child (film)|Wild Child]]'' contains several scenes filmed at Robin Hood's Bay.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2014 |title=Wild Child (2008) – Filming Locations |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1024255/locations?mode=desktop |access-date=9 July 2014 |website=IMDb}}</ref> The 2017 film ''[[Phantom Thread]]'' starring Daniel Day-Lewis features a number of Robin Hood's Bay locations, including the classic interior of the Victoria Hotel and the clifftops above the village.<ref>{{Cite web |title=TV and Film Locations |url=http://www.northyorkmoors.org.uk/visiting/see-and-do/tv-and-film-locations |access-date=21 January 2018 |website=[[North York Moors National Park]] |archive-date=21 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180121184616/http://www.northyorkmoors.org.uk/visiting/see-and-do/tv-and-film-locations |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Missing in Time'', a novel by Catherine Harriott, is set in Robin Hood's Bay and contains references and descriptions of local history, geography and culture.  "Robin Hood's Bay" is a poem by children's poet [[Michael Rosen (author)|Michael Rosen]].

The ''Bayfair'' newspaper contains news and local information on the village. Wireless Internet access is provided for visitors all around the village by the Bay Broadband Co-operative.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ispreview.co.uk/index.php/2012/05/remote-north-yorkshire-uk-village-of-robin-hoods-bay-gets-faster-broadband.html|title=Remote North Yorkshire UK Village of Robin Hoods Bay Gets Faster Broadband|date=21 May 2012|work=ISPreview|accessdate=30 November 2021}}</ref>

== Media ==
Local news and television programmes are provided by [[BBC North East and Cumbria]] and [[ITV Tyne Tees]]. Television signals are received from the local relay transmitter which transmitted via the [[Bilsdale transmitting station|Bilsdale]] TV transmitter, the relay transmitter is situated near [[Ravenscar, North Yorkshire|Ravenscar]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/Ravenscar|title=Freeview Light on the Ravenscar (North Yorkshire, England) transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|accessdate=9 May 2024}}</ref>

Local radio stations are [[BBC Radio Tees]], [[BBC Radio York]], [[Yorkshire Coast Radio|Greatest Hits Radio Yorkshire Coast]], [[Coast & County Radio]] and [[This is The Coast]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bestradios.co.uk/yorkshire-radio-stations/|title=Yorkshire Radio Stations|date=12 July 2018 |access-date=9 May 2024|archive-date=18 April 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240418150746/https://bestradios.co.uk/yorkshire-radio-stations/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The village is served by these local newspapers:
*''[[Whitby Gazette]]''
*''[[Evening Gazette (Teesside)|Evening Gazette]]''
*''BayTown Chronicle'' [https://bay.town/]

It dates from 1733 and was built for the Winn family on the site of a medieval priory. The Priory and its contents were given to the National Trust in 1953 by the trustees of the estate and Rowland Winn, 3rd Baron St Oswald.

'''Nostell Priory''' is a [[Palladian]] house in [[Nostell]], [[West Yorkshire]], in England, near [[Crofton, West Yorkshire|Crofton]] and on the road to [[Doncaster]] from [[Wakefield]]. It dates from 1733 and was built for the Winn family on the site of a [[medieval priory]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n5BCAAAAYAAJ&q=%22nostal+priory%22&pg=PA215 |title=A Topographical Dictionary of Great Britain and Ireland: Compiled from Local ... |first=John |last=Gorton |page=215 |year=1833 |access-date=3 August 2016}}</ref> The Priory and its contents were given to the [[National Trust]] in 1953 by the trustees of the estate and Rowland Winn, 3rd Baron St Oswald.

==History==
===Monastic history===
The priory was a 12th-century [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] foundation, dedicated to [[Oswald of Northumbria|St Oswald]], supported initially by [[Robert de Lacy]] of [[Pontefract]] and [[Thurstan of York]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.york.ac.uk/media/library/documents/borthwick/samplepages/8.BP111.pdf|title=The Foundation of Nostell Priory, 1109–1153|website=York.ac.uk}}</ref> 
By about 1114, Aldulf, confessor to [[Henry I of England]], was [[Prior (ecclesiastical)|prior]] of a group of [[regular canons]] at Nostell.<ref>{{cite book|author-link=David Knowles (scholar)|first=David |last=Knowles |title=The Monastic Order in England|edition=second |year=1963|page= 229}}</ref> It is probable that [[Scone Abbey]] in [[Scotland]] was founded by monks from Nostell.<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|cat=PLA|num=28192|num2=NO12NW 9.3|desc=Scone Abbey|access-date=20 June 2025}}</ref>

[[John Field (astronomer)|Sir John Field]], the first [[Nicolaus Copernicus|Copernican]] astronomer of note in England, is believed to have studied at Nostell in his youth under the tutelage of Prior Alured Comwn.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.g4fas.net/JohnField.html|title=John Field (1522–1587) of Ardsley, nr Wakefield|website=www.g4fas.net|accessdate=18 June 2021}}</ref>

As part of the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]], the priory was seized and depredated in 1540 and granted to Dr. Thomas Leigh.<ref>Hussey, C. -Nostdl Priory, Yorkshire-1: The Property of tire Trustees of the Late Lord St Oswald', CountryLife
(16 May 1952), p. 1492</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=36270 |title=Houses of Austin canons: Priory of Nostell | British History Online |website=British-history.ac.uk |access-date=3 August 2016}}</ref> Nostell was purchased in 1567 by [[Thomas Gargrave|Sir Thomas Gargrave]], a [[High Sheriff of Yorkshire]], [[Speaker of the House of Commons]] and President of the [[Council of the North]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-BgHAAAAYAAJ&q=%22thomas+gargrave%22+levett&pg=PA2 |title=Chapters in the History of Yorkshire: Being a Collection of Original Letters ... |first=James Joel |last=Cartwright |page=2 |year=1872 |access-date=3 August 2016}}</ref> from [[James Blount, 6th Baron Mountjoy|the 6th Baron Mountjoy]] for £3,560.<ref>{{ cite book |title=The House of Commons:1509–1558 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u_eIrJpc_T0C&q=elizabeth+levett+normanton&pg=PA188 |last=Bindoff |first=Stanley T. |publisher=Secker & Warburg |location=London |year=1982 |isbn = 9780436042829}}</ref> In 1613 it was purchased by William Ireland who, in 1629, sold the estate to [[Sir John Wolstenholme, 1st Baronet]], for £10,000. Nostell was then bought by the Winns from Wolstenholme<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nostell-priory-and-parkland/features/a-timeline-of-nostell-priory|title=A timeline of Nostell|website=National Trust|accessdate=18 June 2021}}</ref> after the Wolstenholme family were bankrupted by debts they incurred to provide finance for the Royalist cause.

[[File:Nostell Priory by Morris (1880).jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.3|Nostell Priory in 1880]]
[[File:Self-portrait Hesitating between the Arts of Music and Painting by Angelica Kauffmann.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|Self-portrait, Hesitating between the Arts of Music and Painting, by [[Angelica Kauffmann]]]]
[[File:More famB 1280x-g0.jpg|right|thumb|upright=1.2|[[Rowland Lockey]] after [[Hans Holbein the Younger]], ''Sir Thomas More and his Family'' (Nostell Priory version, 1592)]]
[[File:Nostell Priory Stables.JPG|thumb|left|upright=1.5|Stable block and courtyard]]
{{clear}}

===Later history===
The estate was purchased in 1654 by the [[London]] alderman, Sir Rowland Winn, after its last owner, [[Sir John Wolstenholme, 1st Baronet|Sir John Wolstenholme]], was declared bankrupt in 1650. Construction of the present house started in 1733 and the furniture, furnishings, and decorations made for the house remain in situ. The Winns were textile merchants in London; George Wynne of Gwydir was appointed as [[Draper]] to [[Elizabeth I of England|Elizabeth I]], his grandson, Sir George Winn was created 1st Baronet of Nostell in 1660. In the nineteenth century the family prospered from the exploitation of coal under the Nostell estate, and later from leasing land at [[Scunthorpe]] in [[Lincolnshire]] after [[iron ore]] deposits were found by 
[[Rowland Winn, 1st Baron St Oswald]], in 1858; Lord St Oswald later played an important role in the construction of the [[Trent, Ancholme and Grimsby Railway]] and the development of the Lincolnshire iron industry (from 1864) and steel industry (from 1891).<ref>Armstrong M. Elizabeth (ed.), ''An Industrial Island: A History of Scunthorpe'', (1983)</ref>

The house was built by [[James Paine (architect)|James Paine]] for Sir Rowland Winn, 4th Bt., on the site of a 12th-century [[priory]] dedicated to [[Oswald of Northumbria|Saint Oswald]]. [[Robert Adam]] was commissioned to design additional wings, only one of which was completed, and complete the staterooms. Adam added a double staircase to the front of the house, and designed buildings on the estate, including the stable block. Nostell Priory is home to a large collection of [[Thomas Chippendale|Chippendale]] furniture, all made for the house and commissioned by Sir Rowland Winn 5th Bart and his wife [[Sabine Winn]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/arts/history/ecc/archive/emforum/projects/brieflives/sabinne_winn/|title = Sabine Winn |accessdate=18 June 2021}}</ref> [[Thomas Chippendale]] was born in [[Otley]] in [[West Yorkshire]] in 1718 and had workshops in St Martin’s Lane, London. The Nostell Priory art collection includes ''[[The Procession to Calvary (Bruegel)|The Procession to Calvary]]'' by [[Pieter Brueghel the Younger]], [[William Hogarth]]'s ''[[Scene from Shakespeare's The Tempest]]''–the first depiction in a painting of any scene from Shakespeare's plays–and a self-portrait by [[Angelica Kauffman]], as well as [[Rowland Lockey]]'s copy of the painting by [[Hans Holbein the Younger|Hans Holbein]] ({{circa|1527}} but now lost in a fire) of ''[[Sir Thomas More and Family]]''; this copy was commissioned in 1592 by the More family and came to Nostell in the 18th century, and is said to be the most faithful to the destroyed original.<ref>
{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/960059 |publisher=National Trust |title=Sir Thomas More and his Family (after Hans Holbein the Younger) |access-date=31 March 2017}}</ref>

[[File:John Harrison clock at Nostell Priory.jpg|thumb|right|The [[John Harrison]] clock at Nostell Priory]]
A [[longcase clock]], with an almost completely wooden internal mechanism, made by [[John Harrison]] in 1717, is housed in the [[Cue sports|billiard]] room. Harrison, whose father Henry is thought to have been an estate carpenter, was born within half a mile of the estate. He was referred to as John "Longitude" Harrison, after devoting his life to solving the problem of finding [[longitude]] at sea by creating an accurate marine timekeeper. Known as [[John Harrison#H4|H4]], this chronometer can be seen at the [[Royal Observatory, Greenwich]] in London. 

In May 2007, a set of [[Waring & Gillow|Gillows]] furniture returned to the house after refurbishment. These pieces furnish the [[tapestry]] room, as do a pair of large [[Venice|Venetian]] vases made of wood inlaid with ivory and semi-precious stones.

The Adam stable block has undergone a major renovation and is now open as a visitor centre for the house and parkland. In June 2009 a suite of bedrooms on the second floor was handed to the National Trust. The bedrooms used by the Winns, had never been on public view before. They contain the original contents, including a regency four-poster bed and suite of Victorian [[bedroom furniture]]. Another room open to visitors is the [[butler]]'s pantry, with a display of Winn family silver, in the adjacent strongroom cabinets.

==Grounds==
[[File:Nostell Priory Lower Lake.JPG|thumb|upright=1.3|left|Lower Lake at Nostell Priory]]
[[File:Nostell Priory Obelisk.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|left|Obelisk Lodge at Nostell Priory]]
Nostell Priory occupies 121 hectares (300 acres) of parkland.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nostell-priory/ |title=Nostell Priory and Parkland |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=21 April 2012}}</ref> Within the grounds and gardens are lakeside walks. The main façade of the house faces east towards a grass vista. Leading to the lake on the west side of the house is the west lawn. The parkland has lakeside and woodland walks, views of the druid's bridge and walks to the restored [[Obelisk]] Lodge, a parkland gatehouse, through wildflower meadows. The park was purchased from Lord St Oswald by the National Trust with funding from the Heritage Lottery fund. The grant enabled the trust to acquire pictures, books, and furniture from the family.

To the west of the Middle Lake lies the Menagerie Gardens, completed around 1760 along with a [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] arch entrance.  Built on the site of a medieval quarry, the [[Menagerie]] included a lioness, monkeys, bats and a [[Cockfight|cock pit]], as well as a keeper's lodge and [[Ice house (building)|ice house]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/yorkshire/nostell/menagerie-garden-walk-at-nostell|title=Nostell Menagerie Garden walk | Yorkshire|website=National Trust|accessdate=23 June 2024}}</ref> The Obelisk Lodge was built in the 17th century and inhabited until the late 1950s.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=National Trust|url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nostell-priory-and-parkland/trails/nostell-priory-obelisk-walk |title=Nostell Obelisk Walk| accessdate= 29 December 2019}}</ref> The main lawn and the lower fields to the east of the Priory have been used for various large and small events over the years, however, it was [[Scouting in Yorkshire and the Humber#Central Yorkshire Scout County|"Central Yorkshire Scout County"]] in 2000 which provided a fundamental change to how the grounds could be used. The organisation chose Nostell Priory as the site for its year 2000 "Millennium Camp", which was to attract around 2,500 people from across the Yorkshire Scouting movement. During the 12-month preparation project to create temporary facilities and infrastructure, [[Yorkshire Water]] employee Jon Potter<ref>https://www.linkedin.com/in/jonpotter/ {{Self-published source|date=June 2022}}{{dead link|date=September 2024}}</ref> persuaded his employers to donate/install subterranean high-pressure water mains and stand-pipe points around the entire eastern grounds. This was unprecedented both in terms of a corporate donation and in its benefit to the Priory, which up to that point had been considering how they could self-fund exactly this improvement.

In August 1982 a music festival was held sponsored and organised by [[Theakston's Brewery]]. Two years later another commercial festival was organised by a different group of people. The "[[Peace Convoy#Peace Convoy|Convoy]]" was involved in organising a [[free festival]] next to it. Riot police were mobilised to deal with the free festival element who joined the event and many were arrested.<ref>{{cite web|title=Nostell Priory|url=http://www.ukrockfestivals.com/nostell-priory.html|publisher=ukrockfestivals.com|access-date=20 January 2013}}</ref>

In 2012 the [[BBC]] reported that planning permission had been granted for an operating base for the [[Yorkshire Air Ambulance]]. The site, including a hangar and aircrew accommodation, was operational by summer 2013. It replaced the previous facility at [[Leeds Bradford Airport]] which is north of Leeds.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-leeds-19949837|title=Wakefield base for Yorkshire Air Ambulance helicopter |work=BBC News |date=15 October 2012 |access-date=2 June 2013}}</ref>

4839878.title: Hardcastle Crags
4839878.extract: Hardcastle Crags is a wooded Pennine valley in West Yorkshire, England, owned by the National Trust. Historically part of the West Riding of Yorkshire, it lies approximately 2 miles (3.2 km) north of the town of Hebden Bridge and 10 miles (16 km) west of the town of Halifax. It gave the title to a poem by Sylvia Plath which was included in her 1960 debut collection, The Colossus and Other Poems.

[[Image:Gibson Mill.jpg|200px|thumb|Gibson Mill and the mill pond]]
'''Hardcastle Crags''' is a wooded [[Pennines|Pennine]] valley in [[West Yorkshire]], [[England]], owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]. [[Historic counties of England|Historically]] part of the [[West Riding of Yorkshire]], it lies approximately {{convert|2|mi|km}} north of the town of [[Hebden Bridge]] and {{convert|10|mi|km}} west of the town of [[Halifax, West Yorkshire|Halifax]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/activityandadventure/walkingholidays/8018560/Hardcastle-Crags-West-Yorkshire-Walk-of-the-week.html |title=Hardcastle Crags, West Yorkshire: Walk of the week |website=Telegraph.co.uk |date=22 September 2010 |accessdate=18 January 2016}}</ref> It gave the title to a poem by [[Sylvia Plath]] which was included in her 1960 debut collection, ''[[The Colossus and Other Poems]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Foundation |first=Poetry |date=2023-04-05 |title=The Handwritten Track Lists of Sylvia Plath by Harriet Staff |url=https://www.poetryfoundation.org/harriet-books/2013/03/the-handwritten-track-lists-of-sylvia-plath |access-date=2023-04-05 |website=Poetry Foundation |language=en}}</ref>

==Gibson Mill==
Approximately half a mile along the valley there is a 19th-century [[cotton mill]] called Gibson Mill.<ref>[https://www.visitcalderdale.com/attra-hardcastle-crags Hardcastle Crags and Gibson Mill], ''Visit Calderdale'', accessed on 27 August 2025</ref> The mill was water powered and has been renovated to demonstrate renewable energy sources and a [[sustainable development|sustainability]] strategy. It is surrounded by {{convert|400|acre|km2}} of unspoilt woodland and crossed by {{convert|30|mi|km}} of footpaths. The former cotton mill was one of the first powered mills built at the start of the [[Industrial Revolution]].

Water powered turbines, photo voltaic panels, [[composting toilet]]s, a wood-burning boiler, a wood-burning [[cocklestove]] and locally sourced reclaimed interior materials have gone into making the venture sustainable.

The mill, a grade II [[listed building]],<ref>{{NHLE|num=1226169|desc=Gibson Mill|accessdate=21 November 2020}}</ref> reopened to the public on Saturday, 24 September 2005, and there are exhibits about the mill and its workers.<ref>[http://www.hebdenbridge.co.uk/news/news05/49.html Gibson Mill re-opens], ''HebdenBridge.co.uk'', 26 September 2005</ref>
