8594226.title: Marsden Moor Estate
8594226.extract:
The Marsden Moor Estate is a large expanse of moorland in the South Pennines, between the conurbations of West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester in the north of England. It is named after the adjacent town of Marsden, and is owned and administered by the National Trust to whom it was conveyed in 1955 by the Radcliffe family in lieu of death duties.
The estate covers 2,429 ha (5,685 acres) of unenclosed common moorland and almost surrounds Marsden. Part of it is in the most northern section of the Peak District National Park. The landscape is made up of moorland, valleys, peaks and crags and has long been modified by man. Marsden is at the eastern gateway to the important ancient Standedge crossing of the moors and evidence of transport related archaeological remains dating from pre-Roman times have been discovered close to the great engineering structures of the canal and railway ages. The moors have been a water catchment area since the Victorian era when several reservoirs were built, along with their associated catchwaters in the Wessenden Valley. The Pennine Way and the Peak District Boundary Walk run across the moors (following the same route between Wessenden and Redbrook Reservoirs.
The landscape supports large numbers of moorland birds such as the golden plover, red grouse, Eurasian curlew and twite. The estate, a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest, forms part of a Special Protection Area and is a candidate Special Area of Conservation.
The estate is managed from a base in the old goods yard, adjacent to Marsden railway station, and the old goods shed has been converted into a public exhibition, entitled Welcome to Marsden, which gives an overview of the estate and its history.
The moor has been affected by fires. Dozens of firefighters were required to put out a blaze in 2011. A fire in February 2019, during an unseasonal spell of warm weather, was described by West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service as one of the biggest moorland fires it had ever had to deal with.

13568789.title: Wentworth Castle
13568789.extract:
Wentworth Castle is a grade-I listed country house, the former seat of the Earls of Strafford, at Stainborough, near Barnsley in South Yorkshire, England. It is now home to the Northern College for Residential and Community Education.
An older house existed on the estate, then called Stainborough, when it was purchased by Thomas Wentworth, Baron Raby (later Earl of Strafford), in 1708. It was still called Stainborough in Jan Kip's engraved bird's-eye view of parterres and avenues, 1714, and in the first edition of Vitruvius Britannicus, 1715. The name was changed in 1731. The original name survives in the form of Stainborough Castle, a sham ruin constructed as a garden folly on the estate.
The estate was in the care of the Wentworth Castle Heritage Trust from 2001 to June 2019 and was open to the public year-round seven days a week. Despite massive restoration, the castle gardens were closed to the public in 2017 amidst a funding crisis. In September 2018 it was announced that the National Trust planned to enter into a new partnership with Northern College and Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council to reopen the gardens and parkland to the public. The  gardens and parkland reopened to the public on 8 June 2019.

main.*:
{{Short description|Country house in Stainborough, South Yorkshire, England}} {{for|the similarly named country house in South Yorkshire|Wentworth Woodhouse}} {{Use dmy dates|date=January 2025}} {{Use British English|date=January 2019}} [[File:Wentworth Castle02 2007-08-13.jpg|thumb|400px|right|Wentworth Castle: [[Horace Walpole]] found the south front (finished 1764) evinced "the most perfect taste in architecture".]] '''Wentworth Castle''' is a [[grade-I listed]] [[English country house|country house]], the former seat of the [[Earls of Strafford]], at [[Stainborough]], near [[Barnsley]] in [[South Yorkshire]], England. It is now home to the [[Northern College for Residential and Community Education]]. An older house existed on the estate, then called Stainborough, when it was purchased by [[Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford (1672-1739)|Thomas Wentworth, Baron Raby]] (later [[Earl of Strafford]]), in 1708. It was still called Stainborough in [[Jan Kip and Leonard Knyff|Jan Kip]]'s engraved bird's-eye view of parterres and avenues, 1714, and in the first edition of ''[[Vitruvius Britannicus]]'', 1715. The name was changed in 1731. The original name survives in the form of '''Stainborough Castle''', a sham ruin constructed as a garden [[folly]] on the estate. The estate was in the care of the Wentworth Castle Heritage Trust from 2001 to June 2019 and was open to the public year-round seven days a week. Despite massive restoration, the castle gardens were closed to the public in 2017 amidst a funding crisis.{{cite news|title=Castle gardens close in funding crisis|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-south-yorkshire-39621046|access-date=2 April 2018|work=BBC News|date=17 April 2017}} In September 2018 it was announced that the [[National Trust]] planned to enter into a new partnership with Northern College and [[Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council]] to reopen the gardens and parkland to the public. The gardens and parkland reopened to the public on 8 June 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/projects/the-latest-from-wentworth-castle-gardens|title=Opening date announced|last=|first=|date=|website=National Trust|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=9 January 2019}}{{cite web|url=https://www.barnsleychronicle.com/article/wentworth-castle-gardens-to-reopen-next-weekend|title=Wentworth Castle Gardens to reopen next weekend – Barnsley News from the Barnsley Chronicle|website=Barnsley Chronicle|access-date=10 June 2019}} ==History== The original house, known as the Cutler house, was constructed for Sir Gervase Cutler (born 1640) in 1670. Sir Gervase then sold the estate to Thomas Wentworth, later the 1st Earl of Strafford (of the 2nd creation). The house was remodelled in two great campaigns, by two earls, in remarkably different styles, each time under unusual circumstances. ==First building campaign== [[File:Stainborough (Wentworth Castle) Vit Brit edited.jpg|thumb|left|300px|East front of Stainborough (Wentworth Castle) in ''[[Vitruvius Britannicus]]'' I (1715)]] The first building campaign to upgrade the original structure was initiated {{circa|1711}} by [[Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford (1672–1739)|Thomas Wentworth, Baron Raby]] (1672–1739). He was the grandson of [[Sir William Wentworth, 1st Baronet]], father of [[Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford|Thomas Wentworth]], the [[Bill of attainder|attainted]] 1st Earl. Raby was himself created 1st Earl of Strafford (second creation) in 1711. The estate of [[Wentworth Woodhouse]], which he believed was his birthright, was scarcely six miles distant and was a constant bitter sting, for the Strafford fortune had passed from [[William Wentworth, 2nd Earl of Strafford]], the childless son of the great earl, to his wife's nephew, [[Thomas Watson-Wentworth|Thomas Watson]]; only the barony of Raby had gone to a blood-relation. M. J. Charlesworth surmises that it was a feeling that what by right should have been his that motivated Wentworth's purchase of Stainborough Castle nearby and that his efforts to surpass the Watsons at Wentworth Woodhouse in splendour and taste motivated the man whom [[Jonathan Swift]] called "proud as Hell".Swift, ''[[Journal to Stella]]'', noted by M. J. Charlesworth, "The Wentworths: Family and Political Rivalry in the English Landscape Garden" ''Garden History'' '''14'''.2 (Autumn 1986:120–137) p. 120. Wentworth had been a soldier in the service of [[William III of England|William III]], who made him a colonel of [[dragoon]]s. He was sent by Queen [[Anne, Queen of Great Britain|Anne]] as ambassador to [[Prussia]] in 1705–11 and on his return to Britain, the earldom was revived when he was created Viscount Wentworth and Earl of Strafford in the [[Peerage of Great Britain]]. He was then sent as a representative in the negotiations that led to the [[Treaty of Utrecht]], and was brought before a commission of [[Parliament of Great Britain|Parliament]] in the aftermath. With the death of Queen Anne, he and the [[Tories (British political party)|Tories]] were permanently out of power. Wentworth, representing a clannish old family of Yorkshire, required a grand house consonant with the revived Wentworth fortunes. He spent his years of retirement completing it and enriching his landscape. Wentworth had broken his tour of duty at Berlin to conclude the purchase of Stainborough in the summer of 1708, and returned to Berlin, armed with sufficient specifications of the site to engage the services of a military architect who had spent some years recently in England, Johann von Bodt. who provided the designs.[[Howard Colvin]], ''A Biographical Dictionary of British Architects'', 3rd ed. 1995 (Yale University Press) 1995. s.v. "Bodt or Bott, Johannes von, (1670–1745)". Wentworth was in Italy in 1709, buying paintings for the future house: "I have great credit by my pictures," he reported with satisfaction: "They are all designed for Yorkshire, and I hope to have a better collection there than Mr. Watson."Letter quoted by Charlesworth 1986:123. To display them a grand gallery would be required, for which [[James Gibbs]] must have provided the designs, since a contract for wainscoting "as {{as written|desi|ned}} by Mr Gibbs" survives among Wentworth papers in the [[British Library]] (Add MS 22329, folio 128). The Gallery was completed in 1724.Colvin 1995, ''s.v.'' "Gibbs, James"; see Terry Friedman, ''James Gibbs'' (1984:123–25, 321f, and pl. 124). There are designs, probably by Bodt, for an elevation and a section showing the gallery at Wentworth Castle in the Victoria and Albert Museum (E.307–1937), in an album of mixed drawings which belonged to [[William Talman (architect)|William Talman]]'s son [[John Talman|John]].Lawrence Whistler, in ''Country Life'' '''92''' 1952:1650, and John Harris, in ''Architectural Review'' July 1961, attributed the drawings, which had been annotated in a different ink ''W.T. del. et inv.'' to William Talman. [[Margaret Whinney]] classed them among attributed designs for which there is not adequate evidence, and, finding them too competent and too French for Talman, ascribed them to Bodt (Whinney, "William Talman" ''Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes'' '''18'''.1–2 [January 1955:123–139] p. 136f, figs. 39ab). Her attribution has been followed, e.g. by Terry Friedman, "The English Appreciation of Italian Decorations" ''The Burlington Magazine'' '''117''' No. 873, Special Issue Devoted to French Neo-Classicism (December 1975:841–847) p. 846 note 27. the gallery extends 180 feet, 24 feet wide, and 30 high, screened into three divisions by veined marble [[Corinthian order|Corinthian]] columns with gilded capitals, and with corresponding pilasters against projecting piers: in the intervening spaces four marble copies of Roman sculptures on block plinths survived until the twentieth century.Horace Walpole, who couldn't praise the house and grounds highly enough (''see below'') dismissed the contents of the Gallery: "but four modern statues and some bad portraits" (quoted by [[Rosalys Coope]], "The Gallery in England: Names and Meanings" ''[[Architectural History (journal)|Architectural History]]'' '''27''', Design and Practice in British Architecture: Studies in Architectural History Presented to Howard Colvin (1984:446–455) p. 450. Construction was sufficiently advanced by March–April 1714 that surviving correspondence between Strafford and William Thornton concerned the disposition of panes in the window sashes: the options were for windows four panes wide, as done in the best houses Thornton assured the Earl, for which [[crown glass (window)|crown glass]] would do, or for larger panes, three panes across, which might require [[plate glass]]: Strafford opted for the latter.Remarked on by Hentie Louw and Robert Crayford, "A Constructional History of the Sash-Window, c. 1670-c. 1725 (Part 2)", ''Architectural History'' '''42''' (1999:173–239) p. 188. The results, directed largely by letter from a distance,[[Robert Benson, 1st Baron Bingley]], the Tory politician and amateur architect, may have "looked after" the project in some way (Colvin 1995 ''s.v.'' "Benson, Robert, Lord Bingley"). are unique in Britain. Sir [[Nikolaus Pevsner]] found the east range "of a palatial splendour uncommon in England."Pevsner, The grand suite of parade rooms on the ground floor extended from the room at the north end with a ceiling allegory of ''Plenty'' to the south end, with one of a ''Fame''. Bodt's use of a giant order of pilasters on the front and other features, suggested to John Harris that Bodt, who had been in England in the 1690s, had had access to drawings by William Talman. Talman was the architect of [[Chatsworth House|Chatsworth]], considered to be England's first truly [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]] house. Indeed, there are similarities of design between Wentworth's east front and Chatsworth. Both have a distinctly Continental Baroque frontage. Wentworth has been described as "a remarkable and almost unique example of Franco-Prussian architecture in Georgian England".Colvin 1995, ''s.v.'' "Bodt or Bott, Johann von". The east front was built upon a raised terrace that descended to sweeps of gravelled ramps that flanked a grotto and extended in an axial vista framed by double [[allée]]s of trees to a formal wrought iron gate, all seen in Jan Kip's view of 1714, which if it is not more plan than reality, includes patterned [[parterre]]s to the west of the house and an [[exedra]] on rising ground behind, all features that appear again in ''Britannia Illustrata'', (1730).Noted by Kenneth Lemmon, "Wentworth Castle: A Forgotten Landscape" ''Garden History'' '''3'''.3 (Summer 1975:50–57) p. 52. An engraving by [[Thomas Badeslade]] from about 1750 still shows the formal features centred on Bodt's façade, enclosed in gravel drives wide enough for a coach-and-four. The regular plantations of trees planted [[bosquet]]-fashion have matured: their edges are clipped, and straight rides pierce them.Illustrated in Lemmon 1975 fig. p. 53. All these were swept away by the 2nd Earl after mid-century, in favour of an open, rolling "naturalistic" landscape in the manner of [[Capability Brown]].Brown is not documented as working at Wentworth Castle. ==First earl's landscape== [[File:Stainborough Castle01 bright 2007-08-13.jpg|thumb|left|"Stainborough Castle" an early example (finished 1730) of a mock ruin as an eyecatcher in the landscape; two of four towers remain.]] [[Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford (1672–1739)|Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford]] planted avenues of trees in great quantity in this open countryside, and the sham castle [[folly]] (built from 1726 and inscribed "Rebuilt in 1730", now more ruinous than it was at first) that he placed at the highest site, "like an endorsement from the past"Charlesworth 1986:123. and kept free of trees missed by only a few years being the first sham castle in an [[English landscape garden]].It was preceded Charlesworth noted, only by Sir [[John Vanbrugh]]'s long bastion wall at [[Castle Howard]] and by Strafford's cousin [[Allen Bathurst, 1st Earl Bathurst]]'s "Alfred's Tower" at [[Cirencester Park (country house)|Cirencester Park]], which might have provided the inspiration. For its central court where the four original towers were named for his four children, the Earl commissioned his portrait statue in 1730 from [[Michael Rysbrack]], whom James Gibbs had been the first to employ when he came to England;M. I. Webb, ''Michael Rysbrack'' 1954:161f (dated "c. 1730"); [[Rupert Gunnis]], ''[[Dictionary of British Sculptors 1660–1851]]'', rev. ed., ''s.v..'' "Michael Rysbrack". the statue has been moved closer to the house. A staunch Tory,He was encumbered by [[James Francis Edward Stuart]], the "Old Pretender", with the useless Jacobite title of "Duke of Strafford" in 1722. Lord Strafford remained in political obscurity during Walpole's [[Whigs (British political party)|Whig]] supremacy, for the remainder of his life. An [[obelisk]] was erected to the memory of Queen Anne in 1734, and a sitting room in the house was named "Queen Anne's Sitting Room" until modern times. Other landscape features were added, one after the other, with the result that today there are twenty-six listed structures in what remains of the parkland. ==2nd Earl at Wentworth Castle== The 1st Earl died in 1739 and his son succeeded him. [[William Wentworth, 2nd Earl of Strafford (1722–1791)]] rates an entry in [[Howard Colvin]]'s ''Biographical Dictionary of British Architects'' as the designer of the fine [[neo-Palladian]] range, built in 1759–64 (''illustration, upper right''). He married a daughter of [[John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll]]In 1740, Argyll retired from the political arena in disgust. and spent a year on the [[Grand Tour]] to improve his taste; he eschewed political life. At Wentworth Castle he had [[John Platt (sculptor)|John Platt]] (1728–1810)Platt, a master builder and statuary (he provided the sculptures in the pediment, 1762), was a member of a dynasty of masons with a stoneyard at [[Rotherham]], South Yorkshire (Colvin 1995, ''s.v.'' Platt"). on the site as master mason and Charles Ross ( –1770/75) to draft the final drawings and act as "superintendent"; Ross was a carpenter and joiner of London who had worked under the Palladian architect and practised architectural amanuensis, [[Matthew Brettingham]], at Strafford's London house, 5, [[St James's Square]], in 1748–49. Ross's proven competency in London in London doubtless recommended him to the Earl for the building campaign in Yorkshire.Colvin 1995, ''s.v.'' "Ross, Charles". At Wentworth Castle it was generally understood, as [[James Grimston, 1st Earl of Verulam|James Grimston, 4th Viscount Grimston]] remarked in 1768, "'Lord Strafford himself is his own architect and contriver in everything."Colvin 1995, ''s.v.'' Wentworth, William, 2nd Earl of Strafford" remarks that Walpole and [[William Bray (antiquary)|William Bray]] (''Sketch of a Tour into Derbyshire and Yorkshire'' 2nd ed. 1783:249 (noted in Colvin) confirm Strafford's responsibility. Even in the London house, Horace Walpole tells us, "he chose all the ornaments himself". Walpole singled out Wentworth Castle as a paragon for the perfect integration of the site, the landscape, even the harmony of the stone:
"If a model is sought of the most perfect taste in architecture, where grace softens dignity, and lightness attempers magnificence... where the position is the most happy, and even the colour of the stone the most harmonious; the [[Connoisseur|virtuoso]] should be directed to the new front of Wentworth-castle:Finished sixteen years previously, in 1764. the result of the same judgement that had before distributed so many beauties over that domain and called from wood, water, hills, prospects, and buildings, a compendium of [[Picturesque|picturesque nature]], improved by the chastity of art."Walpole, ''The History of the Modern Taste in Gardening'' (1780).
==Later history== [[File:Wentworthcastleside.jpg|thumb|right|Early 19th century print of the castle showing both the south and east façades]] With the extinction of the earldom following the death of [[Frederick Wentworth, 3rd Earl of Strafford]] in 1799, the huge family estates were divided into three, one-third going to the descendants of each daughter of [[Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford (1672–1739)|the 1st Earl]]. Wentworth Castle was left in trust for Lady Henrietta Vernon's grandson [[Frederick Vernon-Wentworth|Frederick Vernon]], (of [[Hilton Hall]], Staffordshire) whose trustees were [[William Fitzwilliam, 4th Earl Fitzwilliam]], and [[Walter Spencer-Stanhope (1749–1822)|Walter Spencer Stanhope]]. Frederick Vernon added Wentworth to his surname and took charge of the estate in 1816. Between 1820 and 1840, the old chapel of St. James was replaced with the current building and the windows of the Baroque Wing were lowered on either side of the entrance hall. Frederick Vernon Wentworth also amalgamated two ground floor rooms to make what is now the blue room. In July 1838, a freak hailstorm badly damaged the cupola and windows of the house as well as all the greenhouses within the walled gardens, yet this pales into insignificance when compared with the nearby [[Huskar Colliery]] disaster where 26 child miners lost their lives due to flooding following the hailstorm. In May 1853, a freak snowstorm also caused severe damage, particularly to the mature trees within the gardens, some of them rare species from America planted by the 1st and 2nd earls. Frederick Vernon Wentworth was succeeded by his son Thomas in 1885 who added the iron framed Conservatory and electric lighting by March of the following year. The Victorian Wing also dates from this decade and its construction allowed the Vernon-Wentworths to entertain the young [[Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale]] and his entourage during the winters of 1887 and 1889. The estate was inherited by Thomas' eldest son, Captain [[Bruce Vernon-Wentworth]], MP for [[Brighton (UK Parliament constituency)|Brighton]], in 1902. Preferring his Suffolk estates, the Captain put the most valuable of his Wentworth Castle house contents up for sale at auction with [[Christie's]] after the [[First World War]]. The paintings sold at Christie's on 13 November 1919.including the ''Young Knight'' by [[Vittore Carpaccio]], which had lurked largely unnoticed in the collection, with an attribution to Dürer (Alec Martin, "The Young Knight by Carpaccio" ''The Burlington Magazine for Connoisseurs'' '''44''' No. 251 (February 1924:56, 58–59). Bruce Vernon-Wentworth, who had no direct heirs, sold the house and its gardens to [[Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council|Barnsley Corporation]] in 1948, while the rest of his estates, in Yorkshire, Suffolk and Scotland were left to a distant cousin.{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/a2a/records.aspx?cat=199-vwm&cid=0#0|title=Vernon-Wentworth Muniments|work=Access to Archives|publisher=National Archives|access-date=8 July 2011}} The remaining contents of Wentworth Castle were emptied at a house sale,Lancaster & Sons, June 1948. and the house became a teacher training college, the Wentworth Castle College of Education, until 1978. It was then used by Northern College.{{cite web|url=http://www.rotherhamweb.co.uk/gallery/wentworth1/ |title=Quick overview of inheritance history of Wentworth Castle|access-date=17 January 2008}} It was featured in the [[Victoria and Albert Museum]]'s exhibition "The Country House in Danger". The great landscape that Walpole praised in 1780 was described in 1986 as now "disturbed and ruinous" with several listed structures put on English Heritage's at-risk registry. The 2nd Earl's sinuous river excavated in the 1730s was reduced to a series of silty ponds.{{cite news|title=National Trust an option for Wentworth Castle Gardens|url=https://www.barnsleychronicle.com/article/national-trust-an-option-for-wentworth-castle-gardens|access-date=2 April 2018|work=Barnsley Chronicle|date=10 April 2017}}Charlesworth 1986:120, 129. Wentworth Castle Gardens, the only Grade I-listed parkland in South Yorkshire, underwent £20m worth of investment from 2002 to 2017.{{cite news|title=Wentworth Castle Gardens – A restoration tragedy|url=https://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/analysis/wentworth-castle-gardens-a-restoration-tragedy-1-8486307|access-date=2 April 2018|work=The Yorkshire Post|date=10 April 2017}} The Wentworth Castle Heritage Trust was formed in 2002 as a charity with the aim "to undertake a phased programme of restoration and development works which will provide benefit to the general public by providing extensive access to the parkland and gardens and the built heritage, conserving these important heritage assets for future generations." The restoration of the Rotunda was completed in 2010 and the parkland has been returned to deer park. The estate opened fully to visitors in 2007, following the completion of the first phase of restoration, which cost £15.2 million,{{cite web|url=http://www.rotherhamweb.co.uk/gallery/wentworth1/ |title=Wentworth Castle Regeneration|access-date=17 January 2008}} Further restoration was completed in 2014. Wentworth Castle was featured on the [[BBC Television]] show ''[[Restoration (TV series)#First series|Restoration]]'' in 2003, when a bid was made to restore the Grade II* Listed Victorian conservatory to its former glory, though it{{cite web|url=http://www.wentworthcastle.org/view.asp?id=235 |publisher=Wentworth Castle|title= Conservatory|access-date=17 January 2008}} did not win in the viewers' response. Subsequently, the Wentworth Castle Heritage Trust took the decision in 2005 to support the fragile structure further with a scaffold in order to prevent its total collapse. The Trust succeeded in raising the £3.7 million needed to restore the conservatory in 2011 and work began in 2012, with grants from [[English Heritage]], the Country Houses Foundation, the [[Heritage Lottery Fund]] and the [[European Regional Development Fund]]. The Trust completed the restoration of its fragile Victorian glasshouse in October 2013 – 10 years after its first TV appearance the ''Restoration'' series. It was opened by the Mayor of Barnsley on 7 November 2013 and opened to the general public the following day.{{cite web|url=http://www.wearebarnsley.com/news/article/3950/victorian-conservatory-runner-up-in-prestigious-awards|access-date=25 October 2013|title=Victorian Conservatory Runner-Up In Prestigious Awards|work=We Are Barnsley|archive-date=29 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029111836/http://www.wearebarnsley.com/news/article/3950/victorian-conservatory-runner-up-in-prestigious-awards|url-status=dead}} Despite attracting tens of thousands of visitors a year, Wentworth Castle Gardens was forced to close in the spring of 2017. During the closure years a small team of gardeners and a group of community volunteers carried out essential maintenance of the gardens and curated an archive of material about the site's history. In September 2018 it was announced that the [[National Trust]] planned to enter into a new partnership with Northern College and Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council to reopen the gardens and parkland to the public in 2019. On Saturday 8 June 2019 the gardens and parkland were reopened under the care and management of the National Trust.{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-south-yorkshire-48444776|title=Cash-strapped Wentworth Castle Gardens set to reopen|date=29 May 2019|work=BBC News|publisher=BBC|access-date=8 June 2019}} The site is open year-round except for Christmas Day. The Partnership between the National Trust, Northern College and Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council delivers a programme of cultural and environmental events at Wentworth Castle and other sites managed by Barnsley Museums. ==See also== *[[Grade I listed buildings in South Yorkshire]] *[[Listed buildings in Stainborough]] ==Notes== {{Commons category|Wentworth Castle}} {{clear}} {{reflist|33em}} {{coord|53.5243|-1.5188|type:landmark_region:GB|display=title}} [[Category:Buildings and structures in the Metropolitan Borough of Barnsley]] [[Category:Tourist attractions in Barnsley]] [[Category:Grade I listed buildings in South Yorkshire]] [[Category:Country houses in South Yorkshire]] [[Category:Houses completed in 1760]] [[Category:Gardens in South Yorkshire]] [[Category:Historic house museums in South Yorkshire]] [[Category:Folly castles in England]] [[Category:Gardens by Capability Brown]] [[Category:Grade I listed houses]] [[Category:National Trust properties in South Yorkshire]]

The '''Treasurer's House''' in [[York]], [[North Yorkshire]], England, is a Grade I [[listed building|listed]] historic house<ref>{{NHLE|num=1257251|desc=Treasurers House and attached garden walls, gate and gate piers|accessdate=3 March 2019}}</ref> owned by the [[National Trust]], who also maintain its garden.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/treasurers-house-york|title=Treasurer's House, National Trust|last=|first=|date=18 May 2009|publisher=www.nationaltrust.org.uk}}
</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.york.gov.uk/environment/Parks_and_open_spaces/Parks_and_open_spaces_general/formal/Treasurers
|title=Treasurer's House Garden (managed by the National Trust) - City of York Council |publisher=www.york.gov.uk |accessdate=18 May 2009 |last= |first= }}
</ref> It is located in [[Minster Yard]], directly to the north of [[York Minster]].

==History==
The first Treasurer for York Minster was appointed in 1091 when the office was established by [[Archbishop of York]] [[Thomas of Bayeux]], but all that remains of his original house is an external wall which forms part of [[Grays Court, York|Grays Court]] and sections of 12th-century masonry in the present Treasurer's House for which it is uncertain whether they are in-situ or have been reused.  As the controller of the finances of the Minster the Treasurer required a grand residence to be able to entertain important guests.<ref name="historyofyork">{{cite web |url=http://www.historyofyork.org.uk/themes/tudor-stuart/treasurer-s-house |title=History of York: Treasurer's House |publisher=York Museums Trust |date= |accessdate=24 September 2015}}</ref><ref name="COY5">{{cite book|section=The Treasurer's House and Gray's Court|title=An Inventory of the Historical Monuments in City of York, Volume 5, Central|location=London|year= 1981|pages=69–76|via=British History Online|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/rchme/york/vol5/pp69-76|accessdate=27 December 2017}}</ref>

The residence served in this capacity until 1547, when the [[English Reformation|Reformation of the English Church]] brought the job of Treasurer to an end. The last Treasurer surrendered the house to the crown on 26 May and it was granted to [[Edward Seymour, 1st Duke of Somerset|Protector Somerset]] by whom it was sold to Archbishop [[Robert Holgate]]. [[Thomas Young (bishop)|Thomas Young]], Archbishop between 1561 and 1568, and his descendants are responsible for the structure of house as it is today. In the early 17th century the Young family added the symmetrical front and almost entirely rebuilt the house. In 1617, the Treasurer's House played host to royalty when Sir George Young entertained [[James I of England|James I]]. The house then passed through a number of private owners including Lord Fairfax and over time was sub-divided into separate tenements.<ref name="historyofyork"/><ref name="COY5"/>

The house was restored to its present state by [[Frank Green]], a wealthy local industrialist, who between 1897 and 1898 bought each part of the house. He appointed [[Temple Moore]] to restore the house and remove numerous earlier additions. This work was mostly completed by 1900 before Prince [[Edward VII|Albert Edward]], Princess [[Alexandra of Denmark]] and Princess [[Princess Victoria of the United Kingdom|Victoria]] visited in June the same year.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Treasurer's House: History of York |url=http://www.historyofyork.org.uk/themes/tudor-stuart/treasurer-s-house |access-date=2022-08-26 |website=www.historyofyork.org.uk}}</ref> When Frank Green retired and moved away from York in 1930 the house and its contents were given to the National Trust.<ref name="COY5"/> This marked the first time both a private home and its original furnishings had ever been given to the Trust.<ref name=":0" />

The house was built directly over one of the main [[Roman roads]] leading out of [[Eboracum|Roman York]] to the North. During major structural changes, carried out by Green, four Roman column bases were uncovered, one of which remains in-situ in the cellar.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Treasurer's House, Minster Yard, York - Jorvik.co.uk |date=24 January 2013 |url=https://www.jorvik.co.uk/treasurers-house/ |access-date=2022-08-26 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Public access==
Treasurer's House is open to the public for an admission fee, and free to members of the National Trust. The garden and Below Stairs Café are free to enter. Cellar and attic tours are available, depending on the time of year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What's on |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/treasurers-house-york/whats-on |access-date=2022-08-26 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref>

==Roman soldiers apparition==
[[File:Francis Drake b1696.jpg|thumb|Portrait of the antiquary [[Francis Drake (antiquary)|Francis Drake]], on display at the Treasurer's House]]

Several ghosts reportedly haunt the house, including that of George Aislaby, who owned the property in the seventeenth century. However, the most notable haunting is by a group of [[Roman soldier]]s, who have been witnessed in the cellar, firstly by a party guest of Frank Green and then many years later during restoration works carried out by the National Trust.<ref name="JVM">{{cite book|last=Mitchell |first=John V. |title=Ghosts of an Ancient City |publisher=Cerialis Press |ol=13708454M |location=York |pages=53–54}}</ref> In 1953, local 18-year-old apprentice plumber Harry Martindale was repairing pipe work in the cellar, the National Trust having decided to remove the coal-fired [[central heating]] installed by Green. After about four hours of work at the top of his ladder, Martindale became aware of a musical sound, resembling a series of repeated single trumpet-like notes. The sound grew in intensity until, just below his ladder, Martindale reported that he saw a soldier, wearing a [[Galea (helmet)|plumed helmet]], emerge from the wall, followed by a [[Draft horse|cart horse]] and about nine or ten pairs of other Roman soldiers. Martindale fell, terrified, from his ladder and stumbled into a corner to hide. The soldiers appeared to be armed [[legionary|legionaries]], visible only from the knees up, in a marching formation, but were "scruffy". They were distinctive in three ways: they carried [[Scutum (shield)|round shields]] on their left arms, they carried some kind of daggers in scabbards on their right side and they wore green tunics. When they descended to the level of the Roman road, on which Martindale had stood his ladder, he was able to see that they wore [[Caligae|open sandals]] with leather straps to the knees.<ref name="JVM"/><ref name="Laycock">{{cite news|url=http://www.yorkpress.co.uk/news/11559578.Famous_ghost_witness_Harry_Martindale_dies/ |title=Famous ghost witness Harry Martindale dies |newspaper=York Express |first=Mike |last=Laycock |date=25 October 2014 |accessdate=24 September 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.welcometoyork.co.uk/treasurer_haunt.html |title=Welcome to Haunted York - The Treasurer's House. |publisher=www.welcometoyork.co.uk |accessdate=18 May 2009 |last= |first= |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110829014142/http://www.welcometoyork.co.uk/treasurer_haunt.html |archivedate=29 August 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.britainexpress.com/cities/york/treasuershouse.htm |title=Treasurer's House, York |publisher=www.britainexpress.com |accessdate=18 May 2009}}</ref>

The experience so frightened Martindale that it was several weeks before he returned to his job.<ref name="Laycock"/> Many years later, excavations in the city revealed that the descriptions of the soldiers' dress given by Martindale, at first dismissed as anomalous, in fact matched those of soldiers who took over the [[Eboracum|Roman garrison]] in the fourth century.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/by-the-look-of-you-youve-seen-the-romans/ |title='By the look of you, you've seen the Romans!' |access-date=2022-08-26 |website=National Trust |language=en|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220727163059/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/by-the-look-of-you-youve-seen-the-romans |archivedate=27 July 2022}}</ref> During the course of his long life Martindale recounted his experience many times, but never changed any of the details and always refused any payment.<ref name="Laycock"/>

The Treasurer's House was visited in the first episode of the [[Discovery Channel]] television series ''[[Ghosthunters (TV series)|Ghosthunters]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/dna/h2g2/A28278138 |title=BBC - h2g2 - Treasurer's House, York, UK |publisher=BBC |accessdate=18 May 2009 |last= |first= }}</ref>

48978017.title: Yorkshire Coast
48978017.extract:
The Yorkshire Coast runs from the Tees estuary to the Humber estuary, on the east coast of England. The cliffs at Boulby are the highest on the east coast of England, rising to 660 feet (200 m) above the sea level.
The North York Moors National Park extends up to the coastline and traverses 26 miles (42 km) of it between Boulby and Cloughton, taking in the historic fishing villages of Staithes, Runswick Bay and Robin Hood's Bay.
The section of coastline south of Bridlington to Spurn Head is also known as the Holderness coast, from the area of East Yorkshire it adjoins.
In 2016, Natural England announced the creation of a coastal path between Filey Brigg and Newport (Middlesbrough) Transporter Bridge. This will eventually link up with paths all around the coastline of England to become the England Coast Path. The section from Filey to Saltburn is in use as part of the Cleveland Way.
The coastline between the two estuaries was historically made up of the East and North Ridings of Yorkshire. From 1974 to 1996, the coast consisted administratively of Cleveland's Langbaurgh district, North Yorkshire and Humberside. Since 1996, the area has been governed by Redcar and Cleveland, North Yorkshire and East Riding of Yorkshire councils.

==Geology==
[[File:A geological survey of the Yorkshire coast BHL31184044.jpg|thumb|A geological map of the Yorkshire coast. North is orientated to the left top corner of the image. This means that the mouth of the Tees is on the left and the mouth of the Humber on the right]]

As can be seen from the geological map, the Yorkshire Coast is composed of shales, alluviums (sand, clay and gravel), oolites, limestones, mudstone, sandstones, ironstones and chalk. Typically, boulder clay<ref name=":1">{{cite web|title=The Holderness Coast: where land meets sea meets sky|url=http://www.eastyorkshirecoast.com/15-content/explore-the-shore/32-the-holderness-coast-where-land-meets-sea-meets-sky.html?tmpl=component|website=East Yorkshire Coast.com|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref> is the section alongside the North Sea in the East Riding of Yorkshire and has been the most prone to [[coastal erosion]]. ''The Lost Towns of the Yorkshire Coast'' by Thomas Sheppard lists 30 settlements that were lost by the time his book was published in 1912.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Wainwright|first1=Martin|title=Yorkshire is disappearing up to three times as fast as last year|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/the-northerner/2012/sep/24/coastal-erosion-yorkshire-north-sea-lost-towns|access-date=10 February 2016|work=The Guardian|date=24 September 2012}}</ref>

[[Kilnsea]] Parish Church was destroyed by [[Coastal erosion in Yorkshire|coastal erosion]] in 1830. It had been noted that the sea was eating away at the coastline before the last burial in 1823. In 1824, services in the church were stopped and 6 years later, the church and many of the dwellings around it had been lost.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Brandon|first1=David|title=Along the Yorkshire coast from the Tees to the Humber|date=2010|publisher=History Press|location=Stroud|isbn=9780752457321|page=9|oclc=620121229}}</ref>

Erosion rates are now averaging {{convert|3.5|m|order=flip}} per year on the sections between [[Hornsea]] and [[Mappleton]] and from [[Withernsea]] to the south.<ref>{{cite news|title=East Riding Coastal Erosion in pictures|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/gallery/2014/jun/24/east-riding-coastal-erosion-in-pictures|access-date=10 February 2016|work=The Guardian|date=24 June 2014}}</ref> Many towns along the coast have installed defences to stop the sea claiming the land, but in some areas, the sea is taking the land and oftentimes is depositing it further down on Spurn Head.

Both Withernsea and Whitby have used Norwegian rocks as sea defences.<ref>{{cite news|title=Imported rocks boost sea defences|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/humber/4138317.stm|access-date=10 February 2016|work=BBC News|date=1 January 2005}}</ref> The Shoreline Management Plan 2, which covers the coastline from the Tyne to Flamborough Head admits that whilst towns such as Filey, Scarborough and Whitby should be protected, other settlements such as Robin Hood's Bay will see properties lost to coastal erosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Report predicts coastal land loss|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/north_yorkshire/5167896.stm|access-date=10 February 2016|work=BBC News|date=11 July 2006}}</ref> Robin Hood's Bay had concrete sea walls installed alongside its shoreline in 1973, but a report issued in 2014 stated that the structure was coming to the end of its design life.<ref>{{cite news|title='Lives may be at risk if sea defences not fixed'|url=http://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/lives-may-be-at-risk-if-sea-defences-not-fixed-1-6615240|access-date=10 February 2016|work=Yorkshire Post|date=14 May 2014}}</ref>

This stretch of coastline is also famous for the collapse of the [[Holbeck Hall Hotel]] near to Scarborough in 1993. After a prolonged rainfall, water had seeped into the earth which destabilised the ground underneath the hotel causing a landslide. Television cameras managed to capture the building falling onto the shoreline below.<ref>{{cite web|title=Holbeck Hall Landslide Scarborough|url=http://www.bgs.ac.uk/research/engineeringGeology/shallowGeohazardsAndRisks/landslides/HolbeckHall.html|website=British Geological Society|publisher=BGS|access-date=10 February 2016}}</ref>

===Whitby Jet===
Part of the coastal geological make-up in North Yorkshire is [[Jet (lignite)|Whitby Jet]]. Jet is a hard [[Lignite]] mineraloid that was wood from Monkey Puzzle and Chilean Pine trees<ref>{{cite web|title=Whitby Jet|url=http://www.whitbyonline.co.uk/whitbyhistory/whitbyjet.php|website=Whitby Online|access-date=10 February 2016}}</ref> laid down 185 million years ago in the [[Jurassic]] era.<ref>{{cite web|title=About Whitby Jet|url=http://www.yorkshirecoastfossils.co.uk/what%20is%20whitby%20jet.htm|website=Yorkshire Coast Fossils|access-date=10 February 2016|archive-date=13 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160713162341/http://www.yorkshirecoastfossils.co.uk/what%20is%20whitby%20jet.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Jet is found on the beaches in the area and its popularity during the 19th century was down to [[Queen Victoria]] who wore Jet jewelry as part of her mourning dress for [[Albert, Prince Consort|Prince Albert]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Hidden gem: Jet gets set to take off|url=http://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/analysis/hidden-gem-jet-gets-set-to-take-off-1-6995349|access-date=10 February 2016|work=Yorkshire Post|date=14 December 2014}}</ref>

===Petrified forest===
A 7,000-year old petrified forest stretches along the coastline south from [[Hartlepool]] and along Redcar Beach. It was first discovered in 1871 when wild boar tusks and deer antlers were found in the sand. Storms in March 2018 revealed the extent of the ancient forest with petrified tree stumps being exposed to the open air on Redcar Beach when a combination of the storm and low tides removed all the sand from the beach.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Flanagan|first1=Emily|title=Storm reveals forest and creatures|work=Darlington & Stockton Times|issue=10–2018|date=9 March 2018|page=60|issn=2040-3933}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Petrified forest draws crowds|editor-last=Richardson|editor-first=Andy|work=The Northern Echo|date=12 March 2018|page=49|issn=2043-0442}}</ref>

===Dinosaur Coast===
The coastline in Yorkshire is home to some of the world's best Jurassic and Cretaceous geology which has given it the nickname of the Dinosaur Coast.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Pidd|first1=Helen|title=For the best beachcombing in the country, head for North Yorkshire|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2007/aug/21/britishidentity.travel|access-date=10 February 2016|work=The Guardian|date=21 August 2007}}</ref> Fossils can easily be found on the beaches at Whitby, Staithes and [[Runswick Bay]] with Britain's oldest dinosaur bone being found on Whitby beach in 2015. The bone fell out of a cliff face and after detailed analysis was found to be 176 million years old.<ref>{{cite news|title=Britain's oldest dinosaur fossil found on North Yorkshire coast|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2015/jun/01/britains-oldest-dinosaur-fossil-found-on-north-yorkshire-coast|access-date=10 February 2016|work=The Guardian|date=1 June 2015}}</ref> A fossilized footprint of what was described as a 'Jurassic giant', and belonging to a meat eating dinosaur (possibly a [[Megalosaurus]]), was discovered in April 2021. The fossil dates the dinosaur to living around 175 to 164 million years ago.

===Spurn Point===
{{main|Spurn}}
Spurn is a peninsula that extends southwards from the south eastern edge of [[Holderness]]. It is {{convert|3.5|mi}} long<ref>{{cite web|title=Spurn Point|url=http://www.yorkshire.com/view/attractions/hull/spurn-point-665672|website=Yorkshire.com|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref> and in places is only {{convert|50|m|order=flip}} wide.<ref>{{cite news|title=Spurn Point|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/yorkshire/spurn/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130706221635/http://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/yorkshire/spurn/|url-status=dead|archive-date=6 July 2013|access-date=11 February 2016|work=Seven Man Made Wonders|agency=BBC|date=28 October 2014}}</ref> It is continually being eroded by the sea and also becomes a dumping ground for sand, pebbles and rocks washed down from further up the coast.<ref>{{cite web|title=Spurn Point|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/handsonnature/estuaries/spurn_point.shtml|website=Hands on nature|publisher=BBC|access-date=11 February 2016|date=18 June 2014}}</ref> It was reported in early 2016, that the Associated British Ports control tower on the point is being re-located across the Humber Estuary to Grimsby due to progressive deterioration of the point.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Pantry|first1=Lindsay|title=Spurn Point 'deterioration' sparks £5m maritime base move|url=http://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/environment/spurn-point-deterioration-sparks-5m-maritime-base-move-1-7701846|access-date=11 February 2016|work=Yorkshire Post|date=28 January 2016}}</ref>

During the First World War, Skinningrove Iron Works manufactured High Explosives and [[Sulfur mustard|Mustard Gas]]. To help protect it form aerial bombardment, a [[Acoustic mirror|Sound Mirror]] was installed at Boulby (see Military history section).<ref name=":2">{{NHLE|desc=World War I early warning acoustic mirror 60m east of Boulby Barns Farm|num=1020760|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref>

In more recent times, windfarms have been granted permission to be sited off of the coastline with some being obvious from the shoreline (Teesside, [[Humber Gateway]] and Westermost Rough), whilst others (Heron Wind and Njord, Hornsea) are farther out to sea.<ref>{{cite web|title=Offshore Wind Operational Report 2015|url=http://www.thecrownestate.co.uk/media/5462/ei-offshore-wind-operational-report-2015.pdf|website=The Crown Estate|access-date=10 February 2016|pages=6–7|date=April 2015}}</ref> There is also an onshore wind farm at Out Newton near to Easington comprising seven turbines.<ref>{{cite web|title=Out Newton|url=https://www.eonenergy.com/About-eon/our-company/generation/our-current-portfolio/wind/onshore/out-newton|website=Eon|access-date=10 February 2016|archive-date=9 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170409201851/https://www.eonenergy.com/about-eon/our-company/generation/our-current-portfolio/wind/onshore/out-newton|url-status=dead}}</ref>
===Fishery===
{{see also|Yorkshire coast fishery}}
Fisheries have been an important part of the coastline's history which still continues today. Some of the world's best crab, lobster and shellfish is to be found in the waters of the Yorkshire coast.<ref>{{cite web|title=East Yorkshire Coast|url=http://www.eastyorkshirecoast.com/14-content/the-coast-at-work/31-meet-the-fleet.html|website=EYC|publisher=Holderness Flag|access-date=10 February 2016|archive-date=20 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160820212922/http://eastyorkshirecoast.com/14-content/the-coast-at-work/31-meet-the-fleet.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Fishing fleets large and small are located at many of the ports on the coastline with Whitby, Scarborough, Filey and Bridlington being prime examples of ports which historically hosted larger fleets.<ref>{{cite web|title=The history of the Scarborough fishing industry|url=http://www.scarboroughsmaritimeheritage.org.uk/article.php?article=149|website=Scarborough Maritime Heritage|access-date=10 February 2016}}</ref> Bridlington is the largest shell fishing port in the British Isles and exports its catches to the continent, most oftentimes being France, Italy and Spain.<ref name=":1" /> Smaller scale operations also exist such as the lobster and crab fishermen working on the shoreline at Hornsea. In the 20th and 21st century, the Hornsea shell fishermen have been in confrontation with the big oil and gas business along the East Riding section of the coast. They maintain that pipes, outfalls and underground gas storage works have all colluded to put their fishery at risk.<ref>{{cite news|title=Claws are out as crab men fight back|url=http://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/news/claws-are-out-as-crab-men-fight-back-1-2419380|access-date=10 February 2016|work=Yorkshire Post|date=13 June 2001}}</ref>

The North Sea also sees plentiful sailings to and from oil and gas installations for supply.

Many beacons were located on the coast, especially during times of national crisis such as the threat of the [[Spanish Armada]]. The beacons were manned day and night with two people during the day and three overnight. Each beacon consisted of three individual fires with the combination of one, two, or all three being lit signalling the perceived intention of invaders.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Lighthouse Trail|url=http://www.visithullandeastyorkshire.com/thedms.aspx?dms=3&venue=2290156&feature=1|website=visit Hull and East Yorkshire.com|access-date=27 February 2016|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304111326/http://www.visithullandeastyorkshire.com/thedms.aspx?dms=3&venue=2290156&feature=1|url-status=dead}}</ref> For example, one fire might mean enemy ships sighted, two fire that the enemy intended to invade, and all three fires that an invasion was imminent.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Rushton|first1=John|title=Lighting the Holderness beacons for the Spanish Armada|url=http://www.scarboroughsmaritimeheritage.org.uk/article.php?article=28|website=Scarborough Maritime Heritage Centre|access-date=27 February 2016}}</ref>

==Military history==
The coast of Yorkshire has been involved in military endeavours since [[Roman Empire|Roman]] times. Roman signal stations were believed to have been installed at Whitby near to where the abbey ruins are<ref>{{cite web|title=Whitby Abbey|url=http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/whitby-abbey/|website=English Heritage|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> and at Goldsborough near Lythe.<ref>{{cite web|title=North East Coast Rapid Coastal Zone Assessment Survey|url=https://content.historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/nercza-aerial-survey/3929nerczasreportasssurvey.pdf/|website=English Heritage|publisher=EH|access-date=12 February 2016|page=22|format=PDF|date=August 2008|archive-date=16 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160216035150/https://content.historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/nercza-aerial-survey/3929nerczasreportasssurvey.pdf/|url-status=dead}}</ref> The breakwater at [[South Gare]] in Redcar, was installed with gun defences in 1891. These were utilised in the First and Second World Wars.<ref>{{cite web|title=North East Coast Rapid Coastal Zone Assessment Survey|url=https://content.historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/nercza-aerial-survey/3929nerczasreportasssurvey.pdf/|website=English Heritage|publisher=EH|access-date=12 February 2016|page=24|date=August 2008|archive-date=16 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160216035150/https://content.historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/nercza-aerial-survey/3929nerczasreportasssurvey.pdf/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The radio and coastguard stations in Scarborough and Whitby were part of a targeted attack on 16 December 1914 by the German Navy during the [[First World War]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Battles; Raid on Scarborough, Hartlepool & Whitby 1914|url=http://firstworldwar.com/battles/scarborough.htm|website=First World War.com|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> Elsewhere, the stretch of coast between the Tees and the Humber was a dangerous place in the First World War due to the presence of the German [[U-boat|U-Boats]]. The U-Boats were responsible for sinking 220 vessels with torpedoes and mines. Many other ships were suspected of being sunk here but they cannot be accounted for.<ref>{{cite web|title=England's Historic Seascapes: Scarborough to Hartlepool|url=http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archives/view/ehsscarborough_eh_2007/navigationroutes.cfm?CFID=1256646&CFTOKEN=CF8393F7-A185-47CF-ACAE82126D6D58E2|website=Archaeology Data Service|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> Between 1917 and 1918 eight U-Boats were sunk off the Yorkshire coast with 6 sites being known and the last two wrecks sites being located in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|title=U-Boats|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/insideout/northeast/series4/uboats_war_northsea.shtml|website=Inside Out|publisher=BBC|access-date=12 February 2016|date=8 September 2003}}</ref>

The spit of land at Spurn Head was militarised in 1805 during [[Napoleonic Wars|Napoleonic]] times. In 1914 when Britain went to war against [[Germany]], Spurn was upgraded with a [[Spurn Point Military Railway|railway]] being built to bring in supplies and ammunition.<ref>{{cite news|title=World War One: Spurn Point's military relics at sea's mercy|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-humber-26324444|access-date=12 February 2016|work=BBC News|date=28 February 2014}}</ref> The headland was used for military purposes during the Second World War and was finally de-militarised in 1959.<ref name=":3">{{cite news|title=Top 10 secret places in Hull & East Yorkshire|url=http://www.hulldailymail.co.uk/10-secret-places-Hull-East-Yorkshire-pictures/story-26096346-detail/story.html|access-date=12 February 2016|work=Hull Daily Mail|date=28 February 2015|archive-date=13 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150813122223/http://www.hulldailymail.co.uk/10-secret-places-Hull-East-Yorkshire-pictures/story-26096346-detail/story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Sound Mirrors were built at Kilnsea, Boulby and Redcar in 1916.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Grantham|first1=Andrew|title=Kilnsea Sound Mirror|url=http://www.andrewgrantham.co.uk/soundmirrors/locations/kilnsea/|website=Sound Mirrors|publisher=AG|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> The concrete blocks had a hollowed out dish shape that pointed out towards the sea. They were early form of [[Radar|RADAR]] being able to detect ships and aircraft up to 25 miles away.<ref name=":2" />

During the Second World War, the Yorkshire coast was fortified with pillboxes and tank traps on the shoreline<ref name=":3" /> and anti-aircraft and anti-shipping batteries installed at Ringborough. The Ringborough Battery was constructed in 1943 on what was then near to the coast line at East Garton.<ref>{{PastScape|num=915262|desc=Ringborough Battery|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> It has been subject to coastal erosion and most of the former battery site now lies ruined or on the beach. The Royal Air Force installed RADAR and listening sites, bombing ranges and Air Force stations along the coast at [[RAF Goldsborough|Goldsborough]],<ref>{{PastScape|num=1487954|desc=Goldsborough ROTOR station JEX|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> [[Bent Rigg radar station|Ravenscar]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Ravenscar WW2 Radar Station on the Yorkshire Coast|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/yorkshire-coast/features/ravenscar-ww2-radar-station-on-the-yorkshire-coast|website=National Trust|publisher=NT|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> [[RAF Bempton|Bempton]],<ref>{{PastScape|num=1415819|desc=RAF Bempton|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> [[RAF Carnaby|Carnaby]],<ref>{{cite web|title=RAF Carnaby|url=http://www.hullandeastridingatwar.co.uk/index.php/erairfieldss/rafcarnaby|website=Hull & East Riding at War|access-date=13 February 2016|archive-date=13 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313211842/http://www.hullandeastridingatwar.co.uk/index.php/erairfieldss/rafcarnaby|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[RAF Cowden|Cowden]],<ref>{{PastScape|num=915915|desc=Great Cowden Air Gunnery Range|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref> and [[RAF Holmpton|Holmpton]]<ref>{{PastScape|num=916225|desc=RAF Holmpton|access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref>

==Rivers==
Of all the major rivers in Yorkshire, only the [[River Esk, North Yorkshire|Esk]] drains eastwards directly to the North Sea without flowing into the Tees or the Humber estuaries. The [[River Swale|Swale]], [[River Ure|Ure]], [[River Nidd|Nidd]], [[River Wharfe|Wharfe]], [[River Aire|Aire]], [[River Calder, West Yorkshire|Calder]] and [[River Don, South Yorkshire|Don]] all end up flowing through the Humber. Even the [[River Derwent, Yorkshire|River Derwent]], which rises on the eastern edge of the North York Moors and reaches within {{convert|4|mi}} of Scarborough turns westwards and then south to flow out through the Humber.<ref>{{cite web|title=Rivers of the North York Moors|url=http://www.yorkshiremoors.co.uk/nature/rivers.html|website=yorkshiremoors.com|access-date=14 February 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Leyland|first1=John|title=The Yorkshire Coast and the Cleveland Hills and Dales|date=1892|publisher=Seeley & Co|location=London|page=224|chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/yorkshirecoastcl00leyl#page/224/mode/2up|access-date=14 February 2016|chapter=xii The Region of the Upper Derwent}}</ref>

In response to flooding on the Derwent in 1799, a river was carved out from [[Mowthorpe]] to [[Scalby, North Yorkshire|Scalby]] which allows floodwaters to drain to the sea, thereby sparing the riverside further downstream.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Dennis|first1=Ian|last2=Girvan|first2=Johanna|last3=Williamson|first3=Phil|title=Restoring the Yorkshire River Derwent|url=http://www.therrc.co.uk/DesignatedRivers/Yorks_Derwent_Technical_Report.pdf|website=therrc.co.uk|access-date=14 February 2016|page=21|date=June 2010|archive-date=24 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160224184657/http://www.therrc.co.uk/DesignatedRivers/Yorks_Derwent_Technical_Report.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[Sea Cut (Scalby Beck)|Sea Cut]], as it is known, was completed in 1804 and roughly follows the route that waters used to drain eastwards towards the sea before the last Ice Age and the Derwent river headed inland.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Yorkshire Derwent|url=http://www.riverangler.co.uk/the-yorkshire-derwent/|website=River Angler|access-date=14 February 2016|archive-date=22 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160222175808/http://www.riverangler.co.uk/the-yorkshire-derwent/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Beaches===
The coastline plays host to many beaches, be they sandy or rocky. As of 2016, just four of the beaches along the coast have been awarded Blue Flag status; Whitby West Cliff, Scarborough North Bay, Bridlington North Beach and Hornsea.<ref>{{cite web|title=UK Blue Flag Beaches|url=http://ukbeaches.guide/blue-flag/blue-flag-beaches.php?country=UK|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150921200100/http://ukbeaches.guide/blue-flag/blue-flag-beaches.php?country=UK|url-status=usurped|archive-date=21 September 2015|website=UK Beaches Guide|access-date=13 February 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Yorkshire|url=http://www.blueflag.org/menu/awarded-sites/2015/northern-hemisphere/england/yorkshire|website=Blueflag.org|access-date=13 February 2016}}</ref>

Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council have responsibility for one of the longest unbroken stretches of beach in the United Kingdom. This section runs from South Gare to Staithes in North Yorkshire.<ref>{{cite web|title=Beaches|url=http://www.redcar-cleveland.gov.uk/rcbcweb.nsf/Web+Full+List/3501709F1AD598EF802579F1002FF8F1|website=This is Redcar & Cleveland|publisher=Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council|access-date=13 February 2016}}</ref> Surfing and Kite Surfing are popular on Redcar beach.<ref>{{cite web|title=Redcar|url=http://ukbeaches.guide/beach-guide/beach.php?beach=3|website=UK Beaches Guide|access-date=13 February 2016}}{{dead link|date=May 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>
